  • In a recent development, the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital.
  • In a recent development, the pair’s completed route around Baffin Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

In a recent development, the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

In a recent development, the pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

With no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

Industry observers note that “With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

Industry observers note that the paddling portion went rapidly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”.

Recent findings suggest that using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

It has been revealed that postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

In a recent development, “It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they said.

Sources indicate that mcDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Industry observers note that slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

“One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We swiftly packed our boats and got on the water.”.

According to recent reports, in Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”.

Industry News: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio.
  • “I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” notes Talbott, who lives in Logan.
  • Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio. The property, which is owned by a family friend, has rolling hills and steep hardwoods and is scattered with hayfields.

“I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” notes Talbott, who lives in Logan. “I found good deer sign, with lots of buck rubs on trees.”.

Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait. Instead, when the season opened, he just walked the woods, scouting and hunting different locations. He used a lightweight tree saddle and climbing sticks to check areas quickly and quietly.

“I sat in six different trees over 12 hunts, moving according to wind and weather conditions,” says the 26-year-old, who works in heavy construction.

On the morning of Nov. 7, he hunted a pinch point where he knew a few does were bedded.

“But I didn’t like the place and started walking the farm again when I climbed down that morning.”.

It has been revealed that it was the first cold day of autumn, cloudy and with temperatures around 40 degrees. Talbott located a couple of fresh scrapes, and climbed into a nearby tree around 1:30 p.m. to hunt that afternoon. He didn’t see much until about 4:30. That’s when he spotted a big deer headed his way along the field edge.

“I knew he was major, and a shooter, and it all happened very fast.”.

When the buck stepped behind some brush 15 yards from Talbott, he drew. The deer stepped into an opening, and Talbott released his arrow.

Recent findings suggest that talbott saw the deer run about 30 yards and, pouring blood, enter the timber toward a distant hayfield. Then it disappeared over a hill.

“I was shaking uncontrollably when I called my wife, dad, and best friend [Brady Garren] and told them what had happened,” Talbott says. “Dad and Brady got there after sunset to help me look.”.

In a recent development, carrying flashlights, the three men followed a blood trail for about 150 yards. But the trail petered out. Then they heard thrashing in a nearby ravine. Thinking it might be Talbott’s buck, they backed out and called in Triple BC Deer Drone Recovery for assistance.

“They got there with a drone a couple hours later,” indicates Talbott. “They flew the drone to where we last found blood and in just a minute the buck was found in the ravine, but its head was up.”.

It has been revealed that they waited an hour and flew the drone again but saw just a slight movement from the buck. An hour later when they flew the drone a third and final time, they saw the buck was dead.

By then, around 11:30 p.m., more friends had arrived and seven people went into the ravine to help haul out Talbott’s huge buck.

“I knew he was a great buck, but I had no idea he was that significant until I walked up to him,” Talbott says. “I was beyond ecstatic.”.

It was after midnight by the time they field dressed the buck and dragged it 600 yards to the truck. They loaded it and drove to a friend’s cooler.

The next day Talbott’s wife, Alison, took photos before they caped the buck and processed the meat. The buck has 16 points and is an estimated 5.5 years old.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

Recent findings suggest that “My taxidermist states it should score about 190 inches,” says Talbott. “The whole thing is so unreal I can’t explain how I feel. I spent a lot of time there hunting and learning the farm, how to use the wind and where the deer were bedding and scraping … It’s just an incredible experience.”.

Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long fresh route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m).
  • This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5.
  • It has been revealed that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long fresh route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to quickly find a different goal.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

It has been revealed that the team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us latest hope,” Steadman recalled.

It has been revealed that off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, on October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman.

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman.

It has been revealed that “In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”.

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” mentioned Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”.

It has been revealed that A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart.

“The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Sources indicate that summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Recent findings suggest that rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, “Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”.

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:.

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, big hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

#9785. The 11 Best Mid-Priced Hunting Rifles of 2026

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4092 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The 11 Best Mid-Priced Hunting Rifles of 2026

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Long before I was a writer at Outdoor Life, I was an OL reader, and mid-priced hunting rifles were my bread and butter.
  • According to recent reports, A hunting rifle is a significant purchase for most people and narrowing the field can be difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Long before I was a writer at Outdoor Life, I was an OL reader, and mid-priced hunting rifles were my bread and butter. I grew up with modest means, so when it came to buying a hunting rifle, I sought out the best information I could in order to spend my money wisely. I know you appreciate value and an honest evaluation, especially when it comes to hunting rifles.

According to recent reports, A hunting rifle is a significant purchase for most people and narrowing the field can be difficult. Hunting rifles can range from around $350 to north of $7,000, which is quite a staggering spread. All hunters want to find that sweet spot between price and quality. We strive to give you valid information on rifles of every price point from budget hunting rifles to premium custom builds.

This is a comparison of mid-priced rifles, retailing from $700 to $1,500, which captures many of the most popular hunting rifles on the market. That’s because so many hunters are willing to spend a little more for a nicer rifle, but don’t want to throw down on a $2,000 gun. This price block has traditionally included mainstream flagship rifles like the Winchester Model 70 and Remington Model 700, Savage Model 110, and others. It is in this range of mid-priced hunting rifles that the average hunter will likely spend their money.

It has been revealed that mid-priced hunting rifles are typically nice, but without many frills or flourishes. They are general production, standard rifles that are made of good, economical materials with basic stocks and run-of-the-mill triggers. Some at the top end of this price range historically have features like better coatings or threaded muzzles — though with the popularity of suppressors for hunting, threaded muzzles are becoming a upcoming standard.

You’ll see better-quality parts and workmanship on mid-priced hunting rifles than their bargain basement counterparts. Bargain rifles use cost-cutting parts and construction methods to keep prices down. The rifles that cost a few hundred dollars more will usually have nicer stocks, finishes, fit, and more consistent accuracy. The mid-priced hunting rifle is the bread-and-butter standard to which both lower and higher-priced rifles are compared.

The Outdoor Life staff has always strived to present you with the most relevant and practical data for rifle accuracy. At one time, we believed that three-shot groups told us what we needed to know. Then, after seeing too much variability, it became five-shot groups, and averages of large numbers of five-shot groups.

Recent findings suggest that within the last couple years, we have realized that even that doesn’t give us the best information for evaluating or comparing rifles — or knowing what we can expect from them in the field. Based on the statistical and range-tested information that the guys in the lab at Hornady presented in their podcast series beginning with Your Groups are Too Small, we took a fresh look at our accuracy protocol and found it lacking.

We will still present you with five-shot group accuracy data, but we’ve also developed an easy method to take those five-shot groups and compile them into a 20-shot composite, which is a much better representation of how the rifle actually shoots and can be expected to shoot. You can read about how to do that, and some of the benefits, here.

We tested some of the rifles in this story using our old protocol, but as we get to re-test some, and test more current versions of others, we will keep this story populated with the best data that we have for each mid-priced hunting rifle. All rifles were tested with multiple types of quality ammunition. All recorded groups were fired from either bench or prone positions, with front and rear support.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (27 Groups total): 1.96 inches.

20-shot Group Size (Stainless Laminate Model in 6.5 CM tested with Barnes Harvest 140-grain): 1.42 inches.

The Tikka T3X family has a cult-like following, especially here in Alaska. These rifles are affordable, accurate, and dependable. They aren’t ultralight, but aren’t too heavy either. The Finnish rifles have a proven track record and are never a bad option for someone looking for a mid-priced hunting rifle.

The T3X Lite is a sleek and simple rifle. It’s like a budget rifle, only nicer in just about every way. It features a closed-top action and simple two-lug stainless-steel bolt. It has a short bolt throw for a two-lug action, and it’s exceptionally crisp and smooth for its class. The bolt features a metal rear shroud, and the bolt handle is dovetailed into the bolt body.

Recent findings suggest that the T3X platform is also available in threaded models and has great aftermarket support for things like scope rings, stocks, and other accessories. You can get into a base model affordably and use that, or upgrade to your liking.

It has been revealed that the rifle is plain but highlights good craftsmanship and attention to detail. Even the small textured portion of the bolt release button matches the texture pattern of the stock—a nice touch. Overall, the T3X Lite is a very sleek and clean rifle, with no sloppy machine work or tool marks. It’s very well-balanced for an all-around hunting rifle, and lots of models are available in the $700 to $1,500 price range. The only complaint I could come up with is that the blued sample I have has a finish that is very susceptible to surface rust, so I’d opt for a stainless or Cerakoted model.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (16 groups): .79 in.

Average 20-shot Group Size (4 types of ammo): 1.36 in.

Sources indicate that the Browning X-Bolt is a highly popular flagship model rifle, and for good reason. They’re generally accurate, dependable, and come in a variety of configurations. Many of their configurations push them beyond the category of mid-priced hunting rifles, but the X-Bolt 2 Composite can be found at retailers for under $1,200.

According to recent reports, the X-Bolt is a three-lug push-feed action that’s fed from a rotary magazine with a rounded bottom, which sits flush with the profile of the stock. It uses an M-16-style extractor and single plunger ejector. It has a two-position safety on the tang that locks the bolt closed when engaged, but the bolt has an override button to allow the shooter to open the bolt or unload while the rifle is on “safe.” The cheek piece is comfortable, and the pistol grip aids with consistent hand placement and trigger pull.

This rifle is similar in weight to more expensive models like the Speed and Mountain Pro, and lighter than some of their heavier target models. It’s got a black stock and basic blued finish. More expensive models — some of which can squeeze under the $1,500 mark — feature camo patterns and Cerakote finishes.

Recent findings suggest that the Browning X-Bolt has been one of the most consistent factory hunting rifles that we’ve regularly tested over the years. While they do vary a lot in price, a base model X-Bolt 2 like this is one of the best values for rifles in this category.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (37 groups): .952 inches.

20-Shot Group Size (Hornady 143-grain Precision Hunter): 1.13 inches.

Known for their affordable rifles, 9mm carbines, and Glock clone handguns like the PSA Dagger, Palmetto State Armory has a hell of a good rifle in the PSA Sabre 10. I got one of these to test, chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor, and was floored by its accuracy. The PSA Sabre 10 is designed to replicate the M110 service rifle, but at a much lower price point. It’s not very flashy, but includes key quality components like a Magpul PRS Lite adjustable stock, a Radian Raptor charging handle, stainless-steel barrel, and adjustable gas block. The bolt also uses double springs on the extractor and dual plunger ejectors for reliable extraction and ejection.

Read More: PSA Sabre 10 Full Review.

In a recent development, it took me a while to get the ideal bolt speed down — which I manipulated by adjusting the gas system. Eventually, I added a heavier buffer too. I did find that I needed to fine-tune the system any time I switched ammo or added a suppressor. For anyone wanting an affordable, quality AR to hunt with, these requirements are a small price to pay. I shot a lot of different ammo through the Sabre 10, and loads using Hornady’s 143-grain ELD-X were best. This rifle is more accurate than most of the bolt-action hunting rifles on this list. It would be an excellent choice for hunting hogs at night using a thermal scope.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (50 yards)(30 groups): 1.8 inches.

Smith & Wesson got everyone’s attention when they introduced the model 1854 in 2024. We eagerly got a sample chambered in .44 Rem. Mag., which also accepts .44 Special, and were thoroughly impressed with the execution on this rifle. Smith & Wesson not only introduced a fresh platform for the brand, they made one of the nicest production lever guns we have seen. This was following Ruger’s acquisition of Marlin and the Smith can go toe-to-toe with the finest Marlins made.

The initial models of the 1854 were blued and all-weather versions of the same gun, chambered in .44. The stainless version we tested was a smooth-running, reliable workhorse that would excel at shorter distances common to a lot of deer hunters. It also incorporates key modern features such as M-Lok slots on the side of the fore-end, a threaded muzzle, and Picatinny rail for mounting an optic.

It has been revealed that you can check out our in-depth review of the 1854 here. Since its debut, the 1854 roster has expanded to include .30/30, .45/70, .360 Buckhammer, and .45 Colt models, including the blacked-out tactical-styled Stealth Hunter model. These are well-built rifles that will last generations, and they’re a great value.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (12 groups): .63 inches.

Average 20-Shot Group Size (3 types of ammo): 1.07 inches.

Christensen Arms is known for their flagship rifles featuring carbon-fiber barrels and stocks, but in 2025, they introduced the Evoke. This is a simplified, more affordable rifle with a steel barrel and synthetic stock that incorporates modern ergonomics and grip geometry. This step towards simplicity gave us a rifle that comes in under a thousand bucks and has proven to be a reliably accurate hunting rifle.

Industry observers note that we tested and reviewed our first Evoke in 6.5 Creedmoor in 2025, but I’ve also been shooting one chambered in the high-pressure 7mm Backcountry. Editor-in-Chief Alex Robinson has been shooting another 6.5 Creedmoor and used it to kill a whopper bull elk with Federal’s new 6.5 Plus Peak Ammo. The Evoke has earned its place as one our favorite hunting rifles under a thousand bucks.

Recent findings suggest that on this rifle, you’ll see price-appropriate features like a somewhat noisy synthetic stock, but the gun has good coatings and is well protected from harsh weather. Despite its scratchy material, the stock does have great modern ergonomics that make it easier to shoot consistently and features a Picatinny rail on the fore-end for mounting a bipod.

This is one of the best newly introduced hunting rifles for the price, and it’s even available in magnum cartridges like the .375 H&H.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (50 yards): 1.36 inches.

In a recent development, most people think of imported lever guns as little more than a novelty, but don’t make that mistake with Rossi. Their R95 is high quality and all business. The laminated .45/70 model that I tested has a smoother action than many of the older Marlins I have shot, though it does lag a bit behind the newer Ruger Marlins. I tested mine with a variety of loads including factory ammo from Black Hills ammo and Federal, as well as hand loads with bullets from Lehigh Defense and Speer, ranging from 300 grains to 405 grains. It cycled everything wonderfully, no doubt aided by its improved M16-style extractor. This rifle comes with a tall front bead sight and a rear peep, with a long length of Picatinny rail for mounting a red dot or LPVO. It handled heavy-recoiling rounds well, but before I did anything, I would remove all components and add thread locker — I did have some optic base screws loosen during testing.

Read More: Rossi R95 Laminate .45/70 Review.

Industry observers note that this is a modern-featured lever gun that’s ready for a suppressor, but also maintains a nostalgic look. For the price, it’s a really good value, though the receiver flats are a bit over polished, and if I squeeze the fore-end, it has some flex. I strategy on either bedding it or swapping it out for an aftermarket set. If you want to get into a lever gun in the mid-priced hunting rifle market, this is a tough one to beat.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (21 groups): 2.26 inches.

The Winchester Model 70 Featherweight is one of the longest-running mid-priced hunting rifles that’s still in production. The featherweight was first released in 1952, and the signature “Featherweight” stock was introduced in 1982. The rifle has seen some changes, but the current production model has a pre-64-style controlled-feed action that Model 70 fans love.

The Featherweight was a lightweight rifle for its time and introduced in the brand new .308 W.C.F. cartridge of 1952 (what we now know as the .308 Win.). That’s what I tested the current production model in, and with the post-1982 Schnabel fore-end and signature checkering, it’s an authentic Featherweight.

Read More: Is the Winchester Model 70 Featherweight As Good As It Used to Be?

Industry observers note that the controlled-feed action features a two-lug bolt and Mauser-style claw extractor, as well as a coned breech for feeding reliability. It also uses a blade ejector rather than a spring-loaded plunger. The blade ejector ejects cases with a force proportional to how hard the bolt is pulled to the rear. Need to reload in a hurry? Grip it and rip it. On the bench though, you can slowly pull the bolt to the rear and hand-pluck your spent case from the bolt face. Because the claw extractor grabs and controls the cartridge as soon as it’s stripped from the magazine, you don’t have to close the bolt to withdraw the cartridge from the chamber like you do with most push-feed rifles.

In a recent development, the wood stock is warm and comfortable and features good wood-to-metal fit with only a couple uneven spots on my sample. Unlike older models, the stock features bedding around the recoil lug and at the tang to help reinforce the wood and provide a more stable connection. My only complaint with the stock is that it’s slightly thicker and blockier than older model Featherweights, particularly in the grip and around the magazine floorplate.

The metal on the rifle features a nice satin blued finish, and the muzzle has a recessed target crown that’s well-protected. An older Model 70 Featherweight I have possesses only a slightly contoured crown, and the muzzle shows some wear from riding around on the floorboards of a pickup.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (22 Groups): 2.2 inches.

The Howa 1500 is another long-running hunting rifle that has models in the 600-1,200 price range. The Model 1500 has been in production since 1979, and it’s been a staple, affordable rifle for many hunters. I killed my first coyote with a 1500 in .223 that my dad bought when I was a kid, and one of the most accurate rifles I’ve ever owned was a heavy-barreled Model 1500 with a laminated thumbhole stock in .308 Win.

Like many rifles, the 1500 comes in a variety of configurations and price ranges—including carbon-fiber barrels and high-end stocks. One of the base models that fits this category perfectly is the Kuiu Verde in .308 Win. The rifle features a tactical gray Cerakote finish, sporter-weight barrel, and a Hogue Kuiu-camo stock with a wide fore-end, meaty grip, and soft recoil pad.

Industry observers note that the Howa Model 1500 action is a simple two-lug push-feed action—much like the Remington 700. Unlike the 700, it features an M-16-style extractor, but does have a single plunger ejector on the bolt face. The recoil lug is machined into the action, and Howa’s trigger group is attached to the action with a single Allen screw.

Industry observers note that sitting in the stock, the barrel channel is even, and the barrel is free floated completely back to the receiver. The stock is beefy, but comfortable to shoot. It has a wide fore-end, and a thick, nearly vertical grip which makes a perpendicular pull on the trigger easy.

Industry observers note that the barrel has a slightly recessed crown, and the muzzle is threaded, although it’s notable that the thread pitch is ½-inch x 28 (a threading that is most common with .22-caliber chamberings) rather than the more common 5/8-inch x 24. The muzzle is ready to be fitted with either a brake or suppressor. Because the barrel is a relatively light sporter weight, expect major point-of-impact shifts when adding a can.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (29 groups): .866 inches.

Average 20-shot Group Size (9 types of ammo): 1.32 inches.

According to recent reports, the Savage Model 110 is a stalwart of the mid-priced hunting rifle category and has been since its introduction in 1963. In fact, it was one of the major competitors that pushed Winchester to adopt a push-feed design for the Model 70 in 1964, according to Jack O’Connor’s writings at the time.

The Model 110 is a simple push-feed, bolt-action rifle that features a second set of lugs behind the forward set. This could still be considered a two-lug bolt because only the forward lugs rotate and lock into the receiver, but the rear ones spin freely around the bolt body and remain in the raceways while the bolt is locked into battery. The bolt handle is cast, and the bolt features a small plunger ejector and an extractor that’s fitted into the right-hand lug (something the push-feed Winchester Model 70 used as well).

The Savage Model 110 is a hunting rifle that was designed to be affordable and accurate, and it carries a reputation for both. The Model 110 Storm that I tested features a stainless-steel receiver and barrel, and a detachable 4-round magazine. I like the design of the magazine because it’s durable, but I did notice that the stainless-finish bottom plate has picked up some surface spot rusting simply from the ambient humidity. The loaded magazine takes firm pressure to insert into the rifle, but it springs free with authority when the magazine release is pressed.

According to recent reports, the rifle features a 3-position tang safety that locks the bolt in its most rearward position. It also uses Savage’s Accutrigger—a user-adjustable trigger with a center safety tab. It’s a well-liked and crisp-breaking trigger that certainly aids with the shootability of the rifle.

Sources indicate that the Trail Hunter Lite model features a fluted barrel that weighs less than the Trail Hunter model that features a pretty heavy barrel. It’s not an ultralight gun, but on par with many other standard bolt-action hunting rifles. This is one of the more affordable Model 110s, and its coatings and stock allow it to hold up to the worst elements. Along with its accuracy, these make it a wonderful value.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (15 groups): 1.96 inches.

In a recent development, if you notice the resemblance between the Weatherby Vanguard series and the Howa 1500, it’s because they are very similar. Howa makes the barreled actions for the Vanguard line, though Weatherby finishes them in Sheridan, Wyo. by adding the stock, trigger, barrel fluting, finishes, etc. The Vanguard series was introduced in 1970 to offer a lower-priced option than the premium Mark V line, and firmly fits the bill for a quality mid-priced hunting rifle.

Like the Model 1500, the Vanguard is a two-lug push-feed action—nearly identical except for a few differences. One is that the Vanguard’s bolt features three small gas vent holes that are visible on the ejecting side when the bolt is closed. The Model 1500 only has the forward hole. Additionally, the Model 1500 has three larger vent holes in the bolt body that point down towards the magazine when the bolt is closed. The Vanguard only has one.

Sources indicate that the Vanguard First Lite features a relatively slender, high-quality synthetic stock. The fore-end is slightly widened at the bottom with a slimming taper closer to the barrel. The Monte Carlo comb provides a comfortable and firm cheek weld, and the subtle texturing on the grip and fore-end make the rifle easy to handle and hold. The stock is finished with First Lite Cipher camouflage pattern.

Recent findings suggest that one notable feature is the rifle’s Cerakote finish, which is even, good-looking, and done in-house at their Sheridan, Wyoming factory. The rifle includes both a slim radial muzzle brake and thread protector—both machined to fit the barrel profile perfectly. The fit is precise, and it’s hard to see the seam when the muzzle brake or thread protector are tightened.

In a recent development, in an apples-to-apples comparison, it’s probably not fair to shoot a fluted, sporter-weight 6.5-300 Wby Mag. against similar-class rifles in .308 Win. The 6.5-300 is an incredibly fast, flat-shooting cartridge, but it will heat up a barrel quickly and is generally much less forgiving than cartridges like the .308 Win. and 6.5 Creedmoor. However, the only sample Weatherby had available at the time was chambered for 6.5-300, and I was excited to see how it would fare. The rifle held its own.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (29 groups): 1.28 inches.

In a recent development, new for 2022, the CZ 600 series was a complete divergence from their previous actions and, following the CZ 600 Alpha, the CZ 600 American is a traditionally-styled wood-stocked version. It has a three-lug, push-feed action that uses a detachable box magazine. Our sample was chambered in .308 Winchester and featured a sporter-contoured barrel, anti-corrosion finish, and a checkered Turkish Walnut stock. It comes with a threaded muzzle, but it’s 9/16×24 rather than the American standard 5/8-24 and will require an adapter for use with most suppressors.

Read More: Full Review of the CZ 600 American.

It has been revealed that the CZ 600 American features an exceptionally idiot-proof adjustable trigger and its heft makes it very comfortable to shoot. The trigger features four adjustment positions similar to those on Sako rifles. It also features an over-sized bolt knob that makes running the short-throw action a breeze. The American isn’t light, but it’s not exceptionally heavy or long barreled either. It would make a great all-around woods rifle for any hunter.

The safety mechanism on the CZ 600 is interesting, as it’s a thru-tang safety that you press down into the tang to disengage, and up from the bottom to engage. The safety locks the bolt, but there is a bolt release button that can be pressed to open the bolt while the rifle is on safe.

The biggest takeaway from accuracy testing mid-priced hunting rifles is that they are generally a step above the budget rifles in accuracy. They will shoot a wider variety of loads with better consistency, but you still might have to spend some time on the bench to find what they really like. Several of the mid-priced rifles have MOA accuracy guarantees for three-shot groups, and I found them all to satisfy their claims.

Recent findings suggest that most rifles in this price block do fall short of the accuracy of premium rifles when it comes to five-shot groups over time, but this probably won’t bother the average hunter. Many people will claim that their mid-priced rifles will shoot just as accurately as any rifle in the $2,000 to $4,000 range, but that’s usually not true. Especially since we’ve started using larger sample sizes (20-shot group aggregates), we see that more expensive rifles are generally much more consistent than budget guns. That stated, All of these are plenty accurate enough, so pick one that best meets your needs and get out and hunt.

The OL editors pick the best deer hunting rifles on the market.

#9784. Te Araroa day 22: Auckland here we come!

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2204 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa day 22: Auckland here we come!

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most of us (me, Lindsay, Sinead, Annabel and Anica) got going at around 7am again, although this time with good reason as we were expecting a bit of a longer day and needed to make a tidal river crossing later.
  • Coffee obtained, it was going to be a good morning!
  • Unfortunately, the day started with a decent road walk of about 7km, which I don’t think any of us had quite registered was coming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

27.5km, Mangawhai trail host to Pakiri Paradise.

Sources indicate that most of us (me, Lindsay, Sinead, Annabel and Anica) got going at around 7am again, although this time with good reason as we were expecting a bit of a longer day and needed to make a tidal river crossing later. The place we were staying was run by people who had previously done TA and provided everything hikers could need, at the very reasonable price of $10 per night. It was a great place to stay, and we walked out of the gate practically right back onto trail. We had been talking about coffee, but didn’t think that anything would be open at that time. But luck was on our side! Literally 50 metres down the street there was a coffee and smoothie van. What a great start to the day. While I was at university I was very much fuelled by coffee, but since then I’ve mostly switched to decaf. But I have been enjoying drinking it again while I’ve been hiking – it gives me a great energy boost, which puts me in a good mood, and I think the negative side effects I’ve experienced previously are reduced by having physical activity to funnel that energy into.

I found a friend when I went to pack away my tent.

Coffee obtained, it was going to be a good morning!

Unfortunately, the day started with a decent road walk of about 7km, which I don’t think any of us had quite registered was coming. Eventually we made it to the beach we would be walking along for the greater part of the day. The signage was familiar to me and I didn’t quite realise why until I registered that it was Auckland Council signage. We had made it to Auckland region! The Northland/Auckland boundary is just south of Mangawhai so that morning, we had completed the first region of Te Araroa. Northland is one of the longest (perhaps the longest?) regions on TA, owing to its long and thin geography. So this was a significant milestone. It was also probably the region I was least looking forward to, yet I loved it. Not every minute, of course, but distance had made my heart grow fonder and I was able to appreciate the beauty of the place with fresh eyes.

The beach looked pleasingly short when we got onto it. That is, until I realised that the headland I could see was not the end of the beach section, but just a blip a few kilometres in. Still, the first section went pretty quickly and soon we were approaching the headland. There were hoards of surfers and foil board surfers, which looked pretty cool! There was also an interesting set up on the beach. Evidently a photoshoot was going on – a bed was set up, and a model posed on it in pajamas while a drone hovered and various involved people fluttered around. I’m sure the six dirty hikers walking through the background didn’t improve their shots!

The first part of the beach, looking towards Te Arai point.

Recent findings suggest that up on Te Arai Point, there were awesome views along the coast. The tracks weren’t super well-marked though, and the route was a bit un-intuitive. I was with Lindsay and Sinead at this point, and eventually we reached a wooded section that popped out on a road back to the beach. Just before the road we stumbled (almost literally) upon Zoe, who was taking a break in what she pointed out might be the last shade for a while. We plopped down to join her, and collectively decided that the rest of the beach necessitated podcasts. I realised I had forgotten to download more episodes when I last had wifi, and scrambled around for something to listen to. I tried an audiobook but I wasn’t really getting into it, and stopped to switch to music and try to find the specific song I had in my head that morning (u + me = <3 by Olivia Rodrigo, in case you were wondering). Tunes acquired, I set off again.

This beach was actually perhaps the most annoying we have had to walk down so far. The tide was fully in at this point and the available area to walk on was soft, slopey, and narrow in places. There was one spot where the waves had created a bit of a cliff about 75cm tall, with very little space between the top of the cliff and the dunes behind. My feet were already wet from a stream crossing earlier, so I just decided to commit and walk in the water below the cliff. Apparently some of the others had taken their chances with the top of the cliff, with fairly unsuccessful results. It was a shame they were behind me, as the descriptions they gave of their falls were pretty amusing!

Walking over Te Arai point, with the surfers in the background.

Sinéad heading to the tidal crossing.

The other notable thing about the beach was the number of dead birds we came across. I really haven’t seen that many before. I hope it isn’t bird flu, which has recently arrived in NZ – perhaps it’s just something to do with the ocean currents that lots of dead stuff washes up there?

At about 11:45 I was hungry. I was going to grab a snack and keep going, but realised I might as well stop for lunch. Who states lunch can’t happen before 12, anyway? I was hungry so I might as well eat properly. I enjoyed my wraps with fresh salad, although I kept dropping things that then got covered in sand. Annabel had told me about these sun-dried tomatoes that come without oil, and I had bought some in Mangawhai. They were great, 10/10 reccommend those. While I was lunching, the others all passed me. After a few more kilometres of walking, I came across everyone sat on the beach eating their (late) lunch. We were nearly at the tidal estuary, which the trail notes remarked could be crossed 90 minutes either side of low tide. It was 2pm, and low tide wasn’t until nearly 5. But the others reckoned someone else had crossed outside of the reccommended window, and we decided to go and have a look.

The butterflies were having a good dance in my stomach as we approached the estuary. I find rivers quite scary, especially when I don’t know how deep they’ll be. We went to the mouth, as that’s where the smaller streams on the beach had been shallowest. But the water here looked quite fast-flowing, so we went further up to a wider, slower bend. It was impossible to tell how deep it was, but at least we wouldn’t get swept away. Sinéad offered to be the guinea pig. She went up to her ankles, then her knees – and then she was basically across. No problem! We all followed without difficulty. Sometimes the trail notes really overstate the difficulty of a thing. I guess it can be deeper sometimes – but we crossed 3 hours before low tide with no bother, when the notes suggested 90 minutes. One of the most valuable pieces of advice I got about TA, which I tell to everyone, came from a couple of NOBO hikers that I picked up near Nelson Lakes last season. They stated that there is a lot of scare-mongering from other hikers, but you have to see for yourself and not put too much stock in what everyone else is saying. And apparently the same goes for the trail notes, too!

Recent findings suggest that the crossing was so fine! Zoe wading across with me, Lindsay, Annabel and Anica waiting. Photo by Sinéad.

Putting shoes and socks back on after the beach.

According to recent reports, we walked up the beach towards a holiday park. We were planning to go a bit further for the day but hoped they would sell us some cold drinks, and maybe fill some water bottles. It was a bit unclear where to go, but there was a man mowing the grass. ‘You lot look like an invading army!’ he called down to us. I suppose the six of us did look like we were plotting how to storm the castle! He invited us to come through the campground and rinse out our shoes and socks. After my sandpaper socks the other day, this was a very welcome invitation. He also said that the notes don’t give good advice about where to cross the river we had just been over. It’s much shallower inland, but the area is home to rare nesting birds, so DOC won’t allow the TA trust to tell people to cross further inland. Personally, I’m happy to wait a bit for the tides if it means not disturbing the birds. But I can see that it’s frustrating for the locals to see people being given less-good safety advice.

It has been revealed that after washing our feet, we all headed over to the shop where we bought ice creams and cold drinks, and checked out the next bit of the route. Everyone kept saying it was really steep, but for some reason I didn’t think it looked too bad on the map. Then I decided to look at a different map app, the one I normally use, and the contour lines looked way denser! I realised that the contours on the TA app are really light and narrow compared to the ones on the map I’m used to, so things don’t look as steep. I guess that could be helpful, in some ways.

It has been revealed that after a while, we headed off down the road. It was a fairly quiet road, and it wasn’t too long before we reached some track. The hill began immediately, and it was steep but not impossible. I ended up passing the others at the first flattish bit and continued on up. The views were pretty good and I felt happy about my fitness. I had a full 4 day resupply on my back but I found the hill ok, and I was able to keep plugging on without having to stop too often. Towards the top, there was a large fallen tree that I had to scramble over. Then I realised I was at the turn off for where we would be staying, and stopped to wait for the others. I watched them all clamber over the tree with varying levels of elegance. I would have taken photos but I didn’t want to walk back down the hill.

You can just see the others lower down the hill.

The house we were staying at was a couple of hundred metres along a side-track. Annabel and I got there first, and the couple came out and introduced themselves, and asked where we were from. Annabel is also from southern England, to which the guy responded that we were both ‘bloody Southerners’; he’s from Yorkshire! The rest of the group arrived and they demonstrated us where we could pitch our tents. It wasn’t as luxurious as the previous night, but we had everything we needed. And, they showed us the view of Auckland city from their garden! This was the first time we had seen the city, and although it still looked very far away, it was cool to know we were getting closer. Everyone was planning to take some time off or visit friends in Auckland, and it’s also the first major city on the route. So it seems to have become a substantial milestone in everyone’s minds.

You can’t see it, but trust me when I say that the Auckland city skyline was visible in this view.

The weather was threatening rain so we pitched our tents, which were soaked from the morning dew still. I managed to snag a decent spot, but some of the others were less lucky and Annabel realised she had pitched her tent in a bit of a bog. Our hosts came out with a packet of scorched almonds, which was very nice of them! A little while later, Xavier demonstrated up. He was at the campsite the previous night, but I didn’t end up speaking to him. Some of the others knew him from before, but I hadn’t met him so I took the chance to introduce myself. Then we carefully prepared dinner on the tables and chairs that kept sinking into the mud, and sat around talking for a while before calling it a night.

#9783. Breaking: Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (389 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (389 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.
  • The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

In a recent development, the small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot.

It has been revealed that macAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill indicates, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

In a recent development, the spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot.

Sources indicate that macAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

#9781. Breaking: Why Mule Deer (Not Whitetails) Are North America’s Greatest Game Animal

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1817 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Why Mule Deer (Not Whitetails) Are North America’s Greatest Game Animal

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve always been a big woods whitetail hunter.
  • So when I moved to Southwest Montana in my late 20s and discovered that the bulk of whitetail hunting there was isolated to wide-open river bottoms and agricultural fields — rather than the surrounding snow-capped mountains and rocky canyons that appealed to my big-woods sensibilities — I was sorely disappointed.
  • It has been revealed that truth be told, I wasn’t all that impressed with mule deer when I first saw them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve always been a big woods whitetail hunter. I grew up in Latest England, where deer hunting meant tracking, still hunting, and roving through endless miles of mixed hardwoods and thick pine forests looking to bag a ridge-running mountain buck. It’s one of my greatest passions and what I truly love to do.

So when I moved to Southwest Montana in my late 20s and discovered that the bulk of whitetail hunting there was isolated to wide-open river bottoms and agricultural fields — rather than the surrounding snow-capped mountains and rocky canyons that appealed to my big-woods sensibilities — I was sorely disappointed. Yet, there was another critter hiding among those picturesque peaks that my local friends assured me would give all the rugged hunting adventure I could ever ask for: the mule deer.

It has been revealed that truth be told, I wasn’t all that impressed with mule deer when I first saw them. They came sedately down to the river when I was fishing and strolled up the driveway to my cabin like demure livestock, as self-assured and unafraid as the cows I saw in the surrounding fields. While I thought they were beautiful and cool-looking animals, they just didn’t spark that same feeling of mystery and lust for adventure that their Eastern whitetail cousins had.

Recent findings suggest that I honestly felt like I would miss my beloved major-woods whitetail bucks when hunting season rolled around, but I still decided to give these bulky, floppy-eared deer a try. Little did I know that by the time my first Western hunting season ended, mule deer would change me as a hunter forever.

One of the interesting things about mule deer is that they’re a relatively newly introduced species. They evolved around the end of the Ice Age when whitetail deer from what is now the Eastern U.S. pushed past melting glaciers to meet and breed with the blacktails of the West Coast, creating a hybridized species of hardy, adaptable deer that soon populated the recently-formed Rocky Mountains. This makes the mule deer a purely North American substantial-game animal that has been shaped and forged by the rugged mountains, plains, and deserts of the West.

Sources indicate that because of the harshness of these environments, mule deer have more to worry about than your average Eastern whitetail. First, they are constantly harassed by predators like wolves, grizzly bears, and especially mountain lions. In Colorado, which has the highest mule deer population of any state at roughly 416,000 animals, it’s estimated that lions kill between 100,000 and 200,000 mule deer each year. This can make mule deer extremely cagey and hard to approach, as they are on constant alert, making them a significant challenge for hunters. It also makes them an incredibly fun and worthy opponent that pushes you and forces you to up your game.

According to recent reports, as mule deer contend with brutal winters, scorching summers, sparse feed, and limited water sources, they have no choice but to be roaming foragers. They require large expanses of wilderness dotted with multiple food and water sources in order to survive.

Whitetails have an average home range of around 300 to 600 acres, where they will often spend their entire lives. Muleys, by contrast, have both summer and winter ranges. These deer can travel as far as 50 miles in just a few days to move from their summer to winter grounds. One particular herd in Wyoming migrates from the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in the northwest corner of the state all the way to southern Wyoming’s Red Desert every year. It’s a 480-mile round trip that makes this herd the farthest migrating big-game animal in the Lower 48.

The result of all this moving and adapting means that you can find mule deer in a variety of different terrains. From mountain forests and grass-rich bottomlands to boulder-strewn canyons and scrubby deserts, anywhere with sufficient forage and water is likely to hold a mule deer or two, so long as it’s the right time for them to be there.

Recent findings suggest that this last point is critical, as mule deer hunting is often a game of “here today and gone tomorrow.” In some ways, it’s similar to chasing migrating waterfowl or even herds of caribou. Once you find them, you often have a short window of time to fill your tag. For hunters who love to witness these migrations, and who enjoy exploring wild and beautiful country, the mule deer is the perfect beast.

There’s a rugged romance to mule deer hunting. It reminds one of those long ago days before trail cams, tree stands, and target bucks infiltrated our hunting culture — a time when going out and harvesting an animal was done with a little know-how, a reliable rifle, and a good pair of boots.

While there are private ranch outfits and other scenarios (especially around agricultural areas) where it’s possible to pattern a single trophy mule deer buck, it’s an entirely different story on the vast public land tracts of the West. On public ground, a mule deer you see in the evening may be ten miles away by the next day. Setting up a stand and waiting for him to come back is pointless. To be a successful DIY mule deer hunter, you typically have to seek the deer out and go after them rather than sit around and wait for them to come to you.

This can turn muley hunting hunting into a drawn-out game of walking and exploring, where you climb up steep mountainsides and crawl over rocks, following tracks and other sign through thick brush and dense timber. It often means hiking deep into the backcountry and studying significant sections of terrain where you might spend hours and even days just watching the landscape and taking your opportunities as you find them. In short, it’s everything deer hunting should be.

Most mule deer aficionados choose the spot-and-stalk method, where you climb to the highest point you can find and then glass the surrounding terrain with binoculars and spotting scopes trying to find an approachable buck. It’s a style of hunting that requires immense patience. You search for food sources and bedding areas and then pick apart the hillsides and brushy valleys trying to make a deer appear before your eyes.

According to recent reports, other mule deer hunters choose to still hunt, tracking the deer through thick timber and snow. This method gets at the very core of hunting, as it requires you to move slowly and quietly through the forest shadows like a predator would, trying to spot a buck before it spots you and bounds away out of sight and out of reach.

Both methods require little equipment beyond a good pair of boots, a sharp knife, an accurate rifle, and a quality pack, which is essential. Because once you hike into good muley territory, there’s a good chance you could come out heavy.

Read Next: The Best Mule Deer Cartridges.

Hunters who do their homework and put in the miles will eventually get opportunities on mule deer. Unlike some other major-game species, which can have sparse or isolated populations, mule deer herds tend to be dense. Their populations do fluctuate, and mule deer have their own conservation challenges, including habitat loss, chronic wasting disease, and other isuses. But these habitual herd animals will often return to good food and water sources year after year, giving knowledgeable hunters some chances at success.

Looking at the numbers in Montana, Colorado, and Idaho, success rates for mule deer hunters seem relatively low, averaging around 10 to 18 percent. The bulk of that harvest comes from areas along migration routes, however, where 25 to 45 percent of hunters are actually successful. Outfitters and guides who set up in these areas, especially those with private land connections, can boast client success rates between 85 and 98 percent. This shows that once you find a lonely corner of land with mule deer in it, you’re likely to find a lot of them. And this is especially true during the rut.

Usually occurring between the second and third week of November in most places, the rut is when mule deer bucks give up their normally solo existence and begin keying in on does. Like whitetails, muley bucks are usually separated from does for most of the year, choosing to travel alone or in small bachelor groups. But once the rut begins and they start seeking out hot does, their habits change.

Recent findings suggest that the rut doesn’t necessarily make them more receptive to calls or scents, like whitetails. But it does mean that so long as you find a few does and keep them in sight, it won’t be long before a buck comes along. Their focus on the doe is often so intense that they’ll ignore everything else around them — including hunters — and if you can avoid scaring off his ladies, you can sometimes make moves in plain sight of a rutty mule deer buck without spooking him off.

Sources indicate that it’ll be a good buck, too. Even younger mule deer sport a branched set of antlers and a heavy body, and after spending so much time hiking and looking for them, every hard-earned muley buck feels like a trophy.

By the last week of my first season hunting mule deer, I was desperate. Those cheeky and seemingly un-spookable deer I had seen grazing along the roadsides and strolling nonchalantly across my front lawn during the summer had disappeared once autumn rolled around. In their place was a wary and flighty animal that seemed to bounce away and vanish into the terrain as soon as I scrambled after them. It was an intensely frustrating experience as the deer always seemed to be just out of my reach.

It has been revealed that I had almost given up when, around last light on the last day of the Montana hunting season, I glassed a small group of deer feeding in a steep canyon. I grabbed my rifle and crawled up the near vertical canyon walls, popping my head over a small crest to see a doe and a nice 4X4 buck looking at me from 150 yards. Shouldering my rifle, I got the crosshairs on the buck’s shoulder and squeezed the trigger just as the deer started to bound away, dropping him in his tracks. As I walked up and held his antlers in my hands, I could tell something inside me was different.

Read Next: Mule Deer Hunting Tips.

In a recent development, nowadays, when I happen across a nice whitetail buck while hunting in the West, I usually won’t even raise my gun. Whitetails will always hold a special place in my heart, but I am now and forever will be a muley man.

#9779. Latest Update: Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (348 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (348 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk.
  • Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida.
  • Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His looks expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards claims, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.
