#9777. Te Araroa day 23: 500km in, have I found my trail legs yet?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2091 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa day 23: 500km in, have I found my trail legs yet?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most of the others left by 7am, but I was a bit slower and wasn’t ready until 7:15.
  • Industry observers note that after a bit of up and down through cow fields, the track went into the bush and I caught up to Lindsay.
  • At the top of the hill, I found Sinead and Xavier by a helipad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

21km, Pakiri Paradise to Dome Cafe.

Sources indicate that most of the others left by 7am, but I was a bit slower and wasn’t ready until 7:15. But not to worry, as it’s a running joke that no matter how much later I leave, I’ll catch everyone up soon enough! I could see Annabel up ahead as I left, but the track went into some bushes and I didn’t see her anymore. The mud began pretty much straight out the gate, and at first I was able to avoid it reasonably easily. But it became apparent that I wouldn’t be able to go around it for much longer, so 15 minutes into the day I committed to the mud and put my feet straight in. The first steps are always the worst, and once your feet are already wet and muddy it doesn’t seem so bad anymore.

Industry observers note that after a bit of up and down through cow fields, the track went into the bush and I caught up to Lindsay. This was interesting, as I hadn’t passed Annabel, and Annabel hadn’t passed Lindsay either. I figured I must have gone past without realising – maybe she was peeing in a bush or had gone the other way around a tree. Not too long after, there was a steep scramble up with some chains – the first (but not last) chains of TA! I don’t think I used them, but I always enjoy those steep scrambly bits. They use different muscles to the regular walking uphill ones, and it’s a mental puzzle as well as a physical challenge.

At the top of the hill, I found Sinead and Xavier by a helipad. We had read about this helipad in the trail notes, and realised that it must be the same one that someone had posted in the TA Facebook group about using as a campsite one night. Unsurprisingly, that post got a number of comments telling him (more or less politely) that camping on a helipad is a pretty stupid thing to do! Fortunately we were not in need of a camping spot, and continued on. The track continued to go up and down, more or less steeply, more or less muddily, for a while.

What a great camp spot that would be.

Well good, because I sure was wearing some.

Eventually I started to hear traffic and surmised I must be getting close to the road. Shortly before the road, there was a steep, wet downhill section that was pretty boggy; and then, hilariously, a wooden bridge over a tiny stream at the bottom. This stream was barely a trickle, while the mud that came before it was at least ankle deep in places. What was the point of the bridge?! The random and pointless boardwalks continued for the last couple of hundred metres to the road. I appreciate the efforts to improve the track, but it really is futile to put a couple of metres of boardwalk in when they are preceded by several kilometres of mud.

It has been revealed that at the road, I took a moment to enjoy my favourite hiker trash snack, mayonnaise on crackers. At this point Xavier appeared, and looked disturbed by my choice of topping. ‘Is that… just sauce?!’ My defence: plain crackers are boring, and I’m carrying the mayo for lunch anyway, so why not add more flavour and calories to my snack?

There was a short section of walking along the main road before I turned off onto a smaller one. On the map it was marked as a gravel road, but this was most definitely surfaced. Oh well. There were some decent views in places, and there was a house offering free filtered water. After not too long, I reached the next bit of track. I felt hopeful when I saw that it had steps, and gravel – maybe the next bit wouldn’tbe so muddy? The steps led up to a kauri dieback cleaning station, where I made a valiant attempt to get the mud off my shoes. It wasn’t very successful though – to make a real difference I would have needed running water. Then the track continued uphill on a gravel road/driveway for a bit. It was only 11am, but when I saw a nice grassy patch by the road I decided to stop for lunch. I wasn’t sure where the next flattish and dryish bit of ground would be in the upcoming muddy forest. I was able to have a nice lunch and dry my tent out, but it was getting pretty warm and by the time I got going again I was feeling full, sleepy and unmotivated.

The track went upwards for a bit more before turning off. I knew that this was where the 500km point was, and after missing the 300 and 400km markers I wanted to make sure I did something for this one. There wasn’t a suitable surface to draw on with my pole, so I gathered some small rocks from the road and wrote 500 with them. I took a couple of photos and headed back into the forest. The mud didn’t seem too bad at first, but became similar to the last bit of track. Up, down, up, down, mud, mud, more mud. Some of the downs were extraordinarily steep, too. Earlier in the day I had been able to enjoy the ridiculousness of slogging through mud for fun, but now my enthusiasm was wearing out. Most of the others had passed me when I was having lunch, but at the bottom of a particularly heinous descent I caught Sinead, who was standing in a stream. ‘We’re really close to the campsite now!’ she said. The campsite she referred to was not where we planned to end the day, but a small one on the way at the end of this section of forest. Still, I was happy to hear we were close, and grabbed some water to filter when I got there. I knew there was a stream crossing just at the campsite, so I believed that Sinead was right and it was just around the corner. However after a bit more walking I checked my map and realised it wasn’t the stream crossing I was thinking of, and I was still about a kilometre away.

Eventually, we did arrive at the campsite. I could see Zoe sitting there with Xavier and one or two other people. Zoe set out early that morning as she was racing to meet some friends who were picking her up at the end of the day, and she must have been on a mission as I hadn’t seen her since the morning! She reckoned she got her trail legs all of a sudden – I would like to know if mine are on the way too, because this section was feeling hard!

In a recent development, also there was Tim, who at first I didn’t recognise, but who I had met at the Ruakaka campsite on the day I arrived. He had been staying with friends and slack packing for a few days. In fact, we had followed him down the beach the previous day – I had seen the hiking pole marks in the sand and the figure in the distance, but not been able to work out who it was.

Lindsay and Anica soon showed up too, but there was no sign of Annabel. We were a bit worried about her, but there wasn’t much to do. At this point, it was about 2:30pm and we still had 7km to do to our intended stop at the Dome cafe. But the temptation to just stay at this perfectly pleasant spot was very strong. I knew I would be annoyed at myself if I stayed, so I washed my shoes and socks in the stream, reapplied my tape, had a snack, and got ready to continue. Someone had noted that track conditions improved from this point, and I sure hoped that was the case otherwise it would be a rather late arrival into camp.

Finally some nice, dry track where I can actually appreciate my surroundings.

My first view of Rangitoto Island in the Auckland harbour.

In a recent development, signs for improved track conditions sure seemed to be good. Across the road, the track went steeply up on a gravel forestry road. It was steep and hot, but at least not muddy. The gradient continued as the road turned into a track, but it was nowhere near as muddy as the previous sections. I was able to make good time, and when the track took a turn into some native bush, I was able to enjoy it. It was a nice bush track, although still of course rather hilly.

Sources indicate that A few kilometres from the end, I reached a trig point. Foolishly, I believed that it would be mostly downhill from here. Boy, was I wrong. There were still at least two substantial hills that just felt never ending. I caught up to Zoe at one point, and finally I came up to a viewpoint where there was a group of day hikers admiring the view, and Tim. I apologised for my smell and asked if it was far to the bottom. It had taken them 20 minutes to get up, which was music to my ears. The track from this point on was all gravelled, with steps. There was one small uphill, which felt big to my tired legs. And finally, I was at the bottom. Zoe’s boyfriend was there, and introduced himself to me, but I was too tired to make intelligent conversation.

The track just after the trig was cool, especially when it was going downhill.

There is space for hikers to pitch tents kindly provided by the old Dome cafe, which is being turned into a house. They provide a small tent area, a sheltered kitchen area, and a hot shower! In a bath tub!! Unfortunately there was no curtain or anything around the shower, and it was a glass door out to the deck. So we had to take it in turns and make sure no one was there before heading round. In the past, I probably wouldn’t have been too keen on this arrangement, but I was so tired and desperate for a shower that I didn’t care. Then I was able to sit in a comfy chair and eat the mammoth dinner I had prepared for myself.

Annabel ended up appearing not too long after me, with Lindsay. It turned out she had got lost very early on when the track turned over a fence and she had continued straight on. She ended up not getting further than 1km on the track by 9:30, so it was very impressive that she had managed to catch up! We all agreed that this was one of the toughest days yet. The mud and the relentless up and down were physically challenging and a bit soul-crushing. Anica had actually gotten injured, and she planned to hitch the next day instead of walking.

The floor lit up in the bathroom. Not quite to my taste, but it’s definitely something!

Recent findings suggest that lindsay and I eat a well-deserved dinner. Photo by Sinéad.

The Dome cafe is just off SH1 north of Auckland, and I remember passing the DOC sign on the way up to Kaitaia. We could hear the road noise from where we were camped, and it was strange after a tough and remote-feeling day to be back so close to civilisation. I thought I would fall asleep rapidly, but unfortunately the ground was not the flattest and I had managed to pitch my tent such that my head was downhill no matter which way I faced. In the end I shoved my rain jacket under my mat by my head, and was able to sleep.

  • I contacted nine current shotgun writers and pressed each one of them to pick a single beloved smoothbore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that most of us fall in and out of love with shotguns throughout the course of our hunting and shooting careers. But as a gun writer, you get exposed to many more smoothbores than the average person because it’s our job to test and shoot every new break-action or repeater we can put hands on and report the results. So, it’s more likely that as a gun writer, the shotgun you cherish today can often be collecting dust in the cabinet tomorrow. Thus, getting a shotgun writer to pick a favorite shotgun is much like asking a cat lady to choose her favorite cat. But, I persisted.

I contacted nine current shotgun writers and pressed each one of them to pick a single beloved smoothbore. Many replied with multiple choices, or wanted to pick a shotgun by pursuit (favorite skeet gun, duck gun, etc.) or hunting season. “Nope,” I said, “you can only have one.”.

In a recent development, several of the writers landed on a sturdy break-action or pump. That’s not surprising, since both platforms are more reliable than auto-loaders due to the simple fact that the guns don’t need to cycle shotshells to function. Gun writers shoot and hunt a lot and so they know that the best gun is the one that goes bang. They also covet the craftsmanship of fine walnut-and-steel smoothbores, often considered a luxury (not a standard feature) in today’s semi-autos. There’s a mix of affordable shotguns that made this list as well, proving gun writers also know a good value when they see one.

Even by his own admission, Snow’s pick for his favorite shotgun is a bit of an oddity. The modern history of Italian shotgun makers is complicated, as there are a number of intermixed families who have been building guns for decades, or more. Among them are the Rizzinis. Without getting too in-depth—as it would take an entire book to unpack the tale—Battista Rizzini has been building guns since 1966, making both high-end and more affordable doubles.

Some years back, Rizzini produced a run of guns for Sig Sauer, including Snow’s favorite, the TR 20 U Aurora. But the business relationship went sideways—as they often do—and you can only find them on the used gun market now.

Sources indicate that snow’s gun is a handsome one, with a color-case-hardened receiver that has some modest scroll engraving, and a nicely finished walnut stock. It is pretty, but not too pretty to take hunting. It has a straight stock, which often doesn’t pair well with an over-and-under, but Snow claims it was one of those guns that he just clicked with. From the first time he shouldered it on a clays course, the shotgun seemed like it couldn’t miss. When you find a gun like that, you don’t pass it up and it has been a consistent companion on Snow’s upland bird hunts since.

A diehard pheasant hunter and clay shooter, it’s not surprising to me Bourjaily picked a hand-made over/under as his favorite shotgun. Bourjaily’s mother came into a small inheritance in the 1960s and used the money to buy her husband a custom Beretta ASEL 12-gauge (we should all be so lucky to marry such a woman). When his father gifted the gun to Bourjaily it was in rough shape and so he sent the Italian-made break-action off to the gunsmiths at Orvis to restore every inch of the ASEL’s steel. For years, it remained his go-to shotgun for pheasant hunting, but Bourjaily uses it sparingly these days. A new ASEL 12-gauge runs around $12,000 and the 20-gauge variant costs nearly double that. But on the used market, this smoothbore can be had for $3,000-$5,000, which is a steal for a custom shotgun.

Sources indicate that “The ASEL is still, I think, one of the better buys on the used market,” Bourjaily claims. “[It’s] an entirely hand-made, high-grade gun you can pick up for a few thousand dollars, although it would cost many times that to have one made today.”.

It has been revealed that roster helped develop the first steel waterfowl loads before the lead ban went into effect in the early 1990s. He still spends a hundred days afield each year, testing lead and non-toxic ammunition for shotshell manufacturers and other public and private entities. Roster has also co-authored several reports on shotshell lethality. He gave up shooting auto-loaders for over/unders in the 1970s because the latter where more reliable and he could select from two different chokes depending on the distance of the bird. The Remington 3200 is the second iteration of the 32, which was discontinued during World Ward II. Both guns can be identified by the lack of side ribs along the double barrels. Roster owns two 3200s and had custom 28-, 20-, 12- (3½-inch chamber), and 10-gauge (3½-inch chamber) barrels built to fit the actions of the guns. He estimates shooting hundreds of thousands of rounds through each 3200 with almost no mechanical concerns.

Recent findings suggest that “I shoot two different Beretta 686s in 20- and 28-gauge for upland bird hunting as well, and load testing,” Roster notes. “Plus, I use a 3-inch .410 Browning Feather XS. I’ve put tens of thousands of rounds through those three guns as well with the same result: zero malfunctions.”.

I’ve always thought the Ruger Red Label is a great value over/under, and every bit the gun that the Browning Citori and Winchester 101 have proven themselves. Ron Spomer, who still chases upland birds in the mountains of Idaho, does too—the 28-gauge Red Label remains his go-to gun. Ruger discontinued the line in 2011 before trying to revive it in 2013, but could not sell enough of the break-actions to keep them in production. Too bad. They are trim, light, and well-made American firearms that you can now buy used for $1,000. Ruger started building the Red Label in the late 1970s to compete with Browning’s Superposed. The Red Label had a four-decade run, but the O/U market became steadily saturated with inexpensive break-actions, which made it tough for Ruger to compete.

“The little wand just fits so well that about all I have to do is lift it and point in the general direction of flapping wings,” Spomer states. “The first year I used it on pheasants, I bagged 23 of 25 roosters we engaged. Several of those fell to my second barrel, but they fell nonetheless.”.

Recent findings suggest that few shooters relish a perfect round of skeet more than Payton Miller. He schooled me for years at the range during our lunch breaks when we worked together in Illinois. I guess the old codger grew tired of 12-gauge recoil, because he ditched an inertia-driven Benelli M1 (that he almost always shot the lights out with) for a single-shot Winchester 37 .410. There were more than 1 million 37s manufactured in 12-, 16-, 20-, and 28-gauge, plus .410-bore. The shotguns have an exposed hammer spur just to the rear of the top break lever, and all barrel is fixed full.

“Why do I like it?” Miller says. “It’s got a bombproof action, it fits me, and is stone simple to operate. Plus, it spares me from having to embarrass myself trying to shoot doubles at skeet.”.

John Gordon was a Texas snow goose guide in the late 1980s and early ’90s when more than 1 million white geese spent winter on the coastal prairie. Thirty years later, he still chases the spring migration of mid-continent snows in the Mississippi Delta and Arkansas. So the CZ Ringneck, a Turkish-made 28-gauge side-by-side, seemed an odd choice for the old snow goose killer, who buys more shotguns in a year than most of us will in a decade. But if the gun fit is right, there’s money in his pocket, and the gun goes bang, Gordon is likely to buy it. The Ringneck debuted in 2005, but fizzled out in less than 10 years. It sits on a boxlock action with engraved sideplates, and has 26- or 28-inch barrels. It was available in 12-, 16-, or 20-, 28-gauge, plus .410.

Industry observers note that “It’s a gun I reach for in the safe many times every fall. [Mine has] 28-inch barrels, single selective trigger, Prince of Wales stock, color-case-hardened receiver… it was the best of the CZ import guns, in my opinion. Why they discontinued it [in 2014] is a mystery to me. The closest model now is the Sharp-Tail. It’s similar, but I still prefer the Ringneck.”.

Sources indicate that one of the most well-traveled hunters in the country, Coogan lived and hunted in Kenya during the 1960s and ’70s. He was also an editor for Petersen’s Hunting in the 1990s when print magazines still had large budgets to send reporters around the world to find stories. Coogan also hosted “Benelli On Assignment,” an outdoor television show that took him across North and South America, as well as Africa. But before all that extensive travel and hunting experience, Coogan grew up with a Winchester Model 42—the .410 variant of the famed Model 12—in hand. As he aged, Coogan acquired each gauge of M12, which was engineered by T.C. Johnson, but based on John M. Browning’s design.

According to recent reports, “I began with a M42 and then as I got older and bigger, moved up to a 20-gauge for doves and quail, and finally the 12-gauge,” Coogan says. “In high school, I took the gun with me, so I could [dove] hunt after class. My first duck with the M42 was a drake green-wing teal that I remember folding like it was yesterday.”.

Yes, there are still double-barreled shotguns handmade right here in the U.S., and Bruce Buck’s favorite is one of the best you can buy: the A10 American Rose & Scroll in 20-gauge. To build this over/under requires 1,300 individual steps. Each component of CSMC shotguns is inspected by multiple gunsmiths, and every shotgun is inspected by the president of the company before it is shipped to the customer. Buck, an accomplished wingshot, international skeet and sporting clays champion, and a former coach at the U.S. Olympic training center, uses his A10 for upland game and shooting sports. As you can imagine, these shotguns don’t come cheap. A 20-gauge starts at $15,000 and rises from there depending on what you want added, such as the quality of the wood, double triggers, fixed chokes, and more.

“It is beautifully built, but the reason that I like it the most is due to its perfect balance,” Buck says. “It does equally well at game birds and sporting clays. It’s good looking, reliable, and a heck of a shooter. You can’t ask for more in a shotgun.”.

Read Next: The Best Workhorse Shotguns That Are No Longer in Production (But You Need to Own).

Sources indicate that john Taylor is one of the last great gun writers from my father’s generation, and it makes perfect sense that Taylor’s most coveted gun is one of this country’s iconic hunting doubles. His A.H. Fox HE-Grade Super Fox 12-gauge was the gun of Nash Buckingham. John Olin of the Western Cartridge Firm famously developed a 3-inch load in 1921 and found that it shot best out of an A.H. Fox double-bored shotgun. So in 1923, America’s first dedicated waterfowl shotgun was built: the Super Fox. Buckingham made the gun famous. His personal gun, Bo Whoop, features in countless Buckingham tales. A 9-pound break-action with lengthened forcing cones, 30-inch over bored barrels, and fixed full chokes, the Super Fox could kill ducks cleanly out to 60 yards (farther in the hands of an accomplished wingshooter) if loaded with Olin’s Super-X copper-plated lead payload. Taylor still shoots the old double gun but has to load it with Kent Tungsten-Matrix or bismuth to kill a ducks now that lead is banned.

“The first Super Fox was shipped to Buckingham, Ensley, Carrigan Company in 1924, when the great Nash Buckingham was a partner in the Memphis sporting goods firm,” Taylor claims. “He heaped praise on the Super Fox. With the balance of a fine bespoke British game gun it’s a joy to shoot with bismuth and Tungsten-Matrix through its extra-heavy, tightly chambered, overbored barrels and even tighter chokes.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Sources indicate that jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

Sources indicate that A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

According to recent reports, he Felt Stuck in Upcoming York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

In a recent development, this Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

In a recent development, men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

In a recent development, two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana. May God’s love, compassion, and mercy fill you, and your family up, then spill over with blessings.

Industry observers note that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton. With a week of successful walking down, we felt another week of slack packing is maybe overly cautious, but (in my opinion) necessary. You can never be too careful when walking long distances. Taking care of injuries early, and not rushing through the recovery, is essential.

Sources indicate that so, our recovery continued along the Waikato River. This is an established walkway for walkers, bikers, and boat racing watchers. Luckily for us, we managed to pick up this section of trail right as the Bridge 2 Bridge races were happening. Slalom skiers, inflatable speed boats, jet skis, and other raceable water craft wizzed past us as we meandered along the paved path.

Recent findings suggest that the trail, post river, takes you through Hamilton, and deposits you just west of town at the Taitua Arboretum. The weather was a bit stormy this week, so in true hiker fashion, we hunkered down, with our fresh British friends, at The Bank for the afternoon. We played cards, drank $4 pints, and enjoyed each other’s company.

Alice and Matt, our latest favorite British couple.

In a recent development, feeling fresh, rejuvenated, and healthy, Maya and I set off from the arboretum. Full packs, flexible walking blueprint, and high hopes, met by towering native trees, proved a great start to the next leg of our adventure.

Sources indicate that the Karamu Walkway is 8.5 km of rolling hills with cool rocks and sheep. Seriously…sheep EVERYWHERE (25,000 to be exactish, according to our friendly trail host). We are just past the lambing season, so all the mama sheep are sheeping about with their lambs. Very cute, except for the fact that all sheep have a severe case of poopy butt, so just don’t look at their rear.

After our time with the sheep, we experienced our first hut. Picture the AMC’s High Mountain hut system, but a bit smaller, no “Croo”, and the huts are included in our trail pass. Mice…nope. Mattresses…yep. Awesome views and everyone staying there is super friendly…absolutely. The climb up and down the Pirongia Traverse was a true test for Maya’s knee, and she left that stretch feeling tired (of course, it was super muddy!), but energized from how great her legs felt. An overall win, and epic section.

Thank goodness for the board walks as you got closer to the hut.

Sunset with Dr. Seuss tree from the hut deck.

While the sections along the beaches, through farmland, and up and over mountains is why walkers walk, Te Araroa throws some lengthy road walks in there. You know, just to keep you grateful for the time spent not on the road. Walk it, hitch it, whatever. It’s your adventure. Maya and I do put our thumbs out when we can, but if we do end up walking it, we are well prepared with high visibility vests, custom made by Maya herself.

We are currently in Te Kūiti letting some weather pass and planning our next section which includes bike riding and canoe paddling. Sounds like a fun switch up giving our walking legs a rest, and our biking legs/paddling arms, some strength. Looking ahead appears to be pretty dang fun. Stay tuned to find out.

P.S. I have been carrying a kite, and her maiden voyage was at Putaki Shelter. Her name is Putaki, Taki for short. I tried to fly her again at the Waitomo Top 10 Holiday Park, but the wind had a mind of its own that day. Let’s see how long she last.

It has been revealed that why do they want it? Weapon lights have become a must-have accessory for defensive shotguns, pistol-caliber carbines and AR-style rifles. You’ll be helping dad complete his next build with one of the best weapon lights out there. This light is exceptionally bright with a focused center beam and good spill. It’s MIL-STD-810H certified for durability and IPX8 certified for waterproofness. It uses a rechargeable 18650 battery and has a lengthy run time for such a powerful flashlight.

It’s a fun and useful optic that is guaranteed to get a great reaction from any outdoorsy dad.

It’s also easy to use with a touchscreen display and app connectivity. Even a luddite will be able to turn it on and start using it right away. The kids can help with changing the color palettes and recording videos.

It’s a comfortable shirt that protects skin from sunburn and keeps you cool through oppressive heat.

According to recent reports, the fit is loose, but not too loose and runs true to size. The hood lays flat when not in use and doesn’t obstruct your peripheral vision when it’s up. The SPF protection prevented burns, even when I spent over 8 hours in the sun. I live in the southeast where the humidity stays above 80 percent all summer, and the Gila wicks the inevitable sweat and keeps me comfortable in triple-digit heat. Another noteworthy feature is that the shirt’s material doesn’t hold odor like some synthetics, so you can probably give dad a hug when he gets home from the lake.

The Gila Pro hoodie is another good option. It has a built in facemask for additional SPF protection or concealment while hunting. Its has a more athletic fit so that it can be worn as a base layer. One of my favorite features is the vented arm pits, which is like having central air built into a shirt.

Every outdoorsman needs a good fixed-blade knife and the Victorinox Venture Pro is a perfect option that won’t break the bank. This is a full-tang knife that’s designed for bushcraft but is versatile enough for camplife, hunting, or anything else your dad likes to do outdoors.

The design of the protruding tang makes it easy to start a fire with the included ferro rod. There’s jimping far forward on the blade’s spine (near the tip), which allows you to choke up on the blade for more control when carving, whittling, or feather-sticking.

The Venture Pro’s handle has a comfortable thumb rest for extra control when using specialized carving techniques like the sternum pull cut, pinch-grip, or power cut.

According to recent reports, it has a polymer handle, which will work well in all weather conditions. The knife clicks positively into its MOLLE-compatible sheath, which also holds a tweezers, ferro rod, and pressurized ballpoint pen.

Trail cameras are practical hunting tools that provide a wealth of insight. But, they’re also a ton of fun. That’s why a trail camera, particularly a cellular trail camera is a fantastic gift. It’s something dad has a practical use for and he’ll have a ton of fun watching photos of deer and other animals appear in the app.

According to recent reports, the Reveal Pro 3.0 won our 2024 trail camera test because of its stellar performance and easy to use app. The key differences between the 3.0 and the 3.0 Pro are that the Pro has an LCD screen and no-glow flash. Both would make excellent gifts for the whitetail fanatic.

In a recent development, if dad loves the sweet smell of hickory smoke in the morning, then this is the perfect gift for him. It’s under $500, small enough to easily move around, and big enough to cook up a feast. It’s ideal for making delicious BBQ, but doesn’t require the work needed to maintain a consistent temperature of a propane or offset smoker. Keep in mind that the max temp is 450 degrees so this grill will be great for low and slow brisket and beer can chicken, but not ideal for searing steaks.

Sources indicate that the Johnny Morris CarbonLite 2.0 is a baitcasting rod and reel setup that will make dad’s day and keep him smiling all summer. It’s a high performance rod and reel that looks as good as it fishes. You can get it in number of configurations, but you can’t go wrong with a 7 foot, medium heavy. If dad fishes a lot of places with thick vegetation, a the 7 foot 3 inch, heavy will allow him to muscle fish out of the cover. Or if he’s a smallmouth angler, the medium or medium light power rods are excellent options.

If the $230 price tag is too steep for your budget, also consider the awesome Bass Pro Shops Pro Qualifier Baitcast Combo, which is $100 less.

Today’s air rifles aren’t Ralphy’s Red Rider or inaccurate pellet guns. They’re powerful and wicked accurate. If dad likes squirrel hunting, hates squirrels, or just likes plinking, the Air Venturi Avenger is a great first reintroduction to the world of airguns. When Jim Chapman did his Air Venturi Avenger review, his rifle shot a 16-shot group at 40 yards that could be covered by a quarter. He also noted that the air rifle was backyard quiet, so it won’t disturb the neighbors. It’s no wonder he chose it as one the best air rifles.

According to recent reports, something any hunter will appreciate is the price of shooting an air rifle, which costs pennies in comparison to the ammo a centerfire or even rimfire uses. Also, at well under $500 it’s a gift a few people can chip in on and provide dad with a ton of fun or a newly introduced hobby.

It was very difficult choosing a knife for this best gifts for dads list, but my selection ultimately landed on the Benchmade Mini Adamas, which won best overall in The Best Pocket Knives review. The Mini Adamas is a tough, rugged blade that is also convenient to carry. Anyone from hikers, anglers, to backcountry hunters will love this pocket knife. Dad will carry his new pocket knife on all his adventures and create new memories with it everywhere he goes. An heirloom piece like this is a special gift that any dad would be lucky to have.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re buying for a dad that loves sharp flying objects, a throwing ax is a fun yet practical gift he’ll love. The Council Tool Flying Fox is balanced for throwing, and sticks in ax targets with ease. But, it is also a great ax for turning logs into firewood and kindling. It makes a great gift because it is an utilitarian tool and backyard fun all in one. At under $60 it won’t break the bank either. If you want to see more ax options check out Drew Conover’s article, The Best Camping Axes.

Sources indicate that the Abel Vaya is a functional work of art. In fact Monte Burke chose it as one the best fly fishing reels in his review. Its performance is stellar, but it also comes in a wide variety of colors and paint schemes. You can even order a custom reel from Abel. And that added touch makes the Vaya stand out as a great gift for a fly fisherman.

It has been revealed that if mosquitoes and gnats are preventing dad from enjoying time outdoors, a Thermacell is a must-have backyard accessory. I’ve tested them extensively while hunting in buggy places and for my best mosquito repellents article. They’re highly recommended and they really do a great job at keeping mosquitoes away.

The EX90 uses a rechargeable battery and just one consumptive refill. While the EX90 isn’t ideal for taking on a backpacking trip or a hike due to its size, it is a great option for RVing, car camping, and the backyard. The device takes 15 minutes to create a protective bubble and will provide protection for nine hours on a single charge. After the heat-up time you’ll have a 20 foot mosquito-free zone.

According to recent reports, if you really love dad or you and other family members want to chip in on something really special, then an heirloom-grade hunting rifle will make an unbeatable gift for any hunter. You might actually make dad cry when he opens the box and finds a rifle with a beautifully figured wood stock.

Industry observers note that buying a Winchester Model 70 Super Grade is the easy decision, but choosing the cartridge it will shoot is a tough one. If dad is a deer hunter you can’t go wrong with the .308 Winchester or the 6.5 Creedmoor. If you live west of the Mississippi and he hunts elk, mule deer, and antelope you might consider going with the 6.5 PRC or .300 Winchester Magnum. If he’s an old school dude, then get him the 30-06 Springfield or .308 Winchester, which are both great for hunting anything in North America. Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief, Alex Robinson, wrote The Case for Newly introduced, Wood-Stocked Deer Hunting Rifles, which makes a compelling case for these timeless rifles.

A hunting rifle, really nice hunting clothing, or a quality knife are all great gifts for a dad that likes hunting.

Dads want a gift that helps them enjoy their hobby and is something they can use for years to come.

A tie is the most common gift and one of the worst gifts for an outdoors dad.

Dad deserves something great this year, and the best gift for dad is one that helps him enjoy his favorite outdoor hobby even more.

#9767. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • It has been revealed that brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their prepares to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

It has been revealed that brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

Indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Recent findings suggest that satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

It has been revealed that american Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

Industry observers note that another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She aims to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also strategy to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

Industry observers note that at least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Industry observers note that satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 blueprint is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

In a recent development, last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni says his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and strategy to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

The Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a latest route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team prepares a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

Sources indicate that the wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and plan to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

#9764. A Risky Summit Push on Everest

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” said Baia.

He states the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health complications. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick new layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

In a recent development, “Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

Sources indicate that “Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

In a recent development, in fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

It has been revealed that after just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

It has been revealed that everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin.

#9763. This Is How the Boomer Generation Shaped Hunting Culture, For Better and Worse

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2662 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

This Is How the Boomer Generation Shaped Hunting Culture, For Better and Worse

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that MY FATHER wasn’t trying to ensure hunting’s future or even create a new hunter when he slid that Savage 24S-E in .22/.410 beneath our Christmas tree in 1971.
  • Still, he had been a boy of the Great Depression, and Dad’s early years had instilled the necessities of marksmanship, fencerow rabbits, and freshly caught bullheads.
  • So on that Christmas Day, Dad drove me outside town, handed me a cardboard box with a Magic Marker bull’s-eye, and told me to put it 30 yards away in the snowy woods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that MY FATHER wasn’t trying to ensure hunting’s future or even create a new hunter when he slid that Savage 24S-E in .22/.410 beneath our Christmas tree in 1971. Dad had quit hunting by the time I was 14, and honestly, he probably wasn’t the best teacher or role model to take me and my three brothers out for rabbits or squirrels. Dad was a crack shot, but he was impatient with hunting and its painstaking tactics.

Still, he had been a boy of the Great Depression, and Dad’s early years had instilled the necessities of marksmanship, fencerow rabbits, and freshly caught bullheads. He enlisted in the Army at age 17, as World War II ended.

So on that Christmas Day, Dad drove me outside town, handed me a cardboard box with a Magic Marker bull’s-eye, and told me to put it 30 yards away in the snowy woods. I then shot, first with the .22 barrel and then with the .410 bore. After we returned home, Dad handed me two latest Hoppe’s cleaning kits, one for rifles and the other for shotguns. He showed me how to swab the barrels with nitro solvent and rub the exterior with light oil.

Sources indicate that his mentoring tasks complete, Dad never again offered another hunting or shooting tip. Even so, with that little gun, my love and obsession for hunting grew. With neither intent nor forethought, Dad had recruited me into hunting’s largest demographic group: white males from families with rural or near-rural backgrounds, born between 1946 and 1964. We baby boomers swelled hunting’s ranks to record numbers by the 1980s, and by 1991 there were still more than 14 million estimated hunters in America.

Recent findings suggest that today, baby boomers are 56 to 75 years old. We’re no longer the majority of -America’s hunters, and our numbers are declining fast. Research reveals folks typically retire from hunting around age 70, which means most of my generation will hang up our bows, rifles, and shotguns for good in the next 10 years, if we haven’t already.

In a recent development, I’m not all that sentimental about this. Baby boomers, after all, didn’t invent hunting. Hunters roamed North America eons before 1946, and they’ll keep roaming long after boomers and our heirs are gone. But my generation’s pending end prompts a question: What, exactly, is the legacy we’re leaving behind?

To answer that question, it’s important to understand how we got started. As kids, we boomers shot BB guns, watched Daniel Boone and Davy Crockett on TV, died daily atop imaginary Alamo walls, and quietly inspected unlocked guns and Remington Peters ammo we removed from our fathers’ Sears, Roebuck gun racks.

We mostly taught ourselves to hunt while envying friends whose fathers, uncles, and brothers also hunted. We weren’t farmers, but we bicycled often to farms and rural woodlots with our recurves or shotguns lashed to our rear baskets. We hunted those places until the landowners shooed us away for November’s gun season, but we returned in December after they again judged us harmless.

By the mid-1970s, we saw whitetail deer herds surge across the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. That explosion occurred promptly and mysteriously.

When I returned home from the Navy in 1980, after missing four years’ worth of deer seasons, I hunted the same woods as before, but I found a far different herd. It seemed the Department of Natural Resources had corralled the results of five years of whitetail reproduction onto one 100-acre woods.

A friend’s dad owned that property and invited me to hunt it after he counted 56 deer on opening morning and shot a -6-pointer before noon. Other friends made claims of 70 to 80 sightings that weekend, 10 times what I’d seen on opening weekend only five years before.

I didn’t shoot any of the many deer I saw in three days of hunting after Thanksgiving 1980, but only because the DNR hadn’t yet invented bonus antlerless tags. Once it did, my freezer was always full of venison.

With so many whitetails on the landscape, hunters adopted a range of beliefs about deer and their management. By the early 1990s, I was passing up yearling bucks regularly, filling free or cheap antlerless tags, and packing our freezers full of six deer each fall. Unfortunately for the herd and its habitat, most other hunters weren’t so eager to shoot does.

With bucks aplenty in the swollen herds, many hunters waited out “their” buck—any buck—and then shot it and went home. Others also ignored does and fawns, as well as yearling bucks, and proudly held out for a “150-class” buck. They pledged allegiance to QDM, and didn’t get the humor when asked if they meant “quantity,” not quality, deer management, which is what they achieved by refusing to shoot female deer.

That combination of surging deer herds and growing boomers sparked the mass production of compound bows, portable tree-stands, and anodized aluminum arrows throughout the 1970s. We boomers weren’t wealthy individually, but collectively we squirreled away fortunes to fund outdoor store layaway programs.

Throughout the 1980s, manufacturers made increasingly fast bows, better-performing bullets, more convincing camouflage, clearer and brighter riflescopes, and warmer and drier hunting clothes. Hunters also began driving ATVs and building increasingly tall and cushy box stands. Hunting media boomed too, with hunters renting VHS tapes and buying three-year subscriptions to a variety of different hunting magazines.

Whitetails kept pace, overwhelming farmers from North Dakota to Georgia.

It has been revealed that hunting gear kept improving and multiplying through the 1990s, with calls, grunt tubes, rangefinders, rattling devices, GPS units, pop-up ground blinds, significant-game decoys, inline muzzleloaders, and much, much more. Boomers were there for it all.

Maybe I’m a product of my generation, as I still use much of that gear today and especially like the better boots and clothes, which keep me happier on stand in all weather. I also admire the straight-​shooting bows and broadheads, which consistently deliver cleaner kills and clearer consciences.

In a recent development, but what about all those gadgets, the ones that Aldo Leopold warned about in the 1940s? Aldo called them “aids to self-reliance, hardihood, woodcraft, or marksmanship, but too often functioning as substitutes for them” and claimed their “aggregate poundage becomes tonnage” when hunters go afield.

Industry observers note that I hold no man in higher regard than Leopold, a member of the Lost Generation, but he overstated things. Yes, hunting’s gadgeteers are making more toys than ever 75 years post-Leopold, but hunters often limit their “tonnage,” promptly abandoning gear that is useless. Also, I haven’t found much evidence that our gadgetry provides an unfair advantage over the game we hunt or makes it difficult for game agencies to regulate harvests.

Recent findings suggest that we boomers excelled at creating and maintaining hunting gear, but we flopped at creating and sustaining upcoming hunters. As early as the late 1980s, industry analysts, university sociologists, and wildlife agency administrators knew our children weren’t following us afield at the pace we’d once set. When demographers plotted hunters’ birth years and projected them on graphs, the baby boomer bulge moved like a basketball through a python. What would happen when hunting’s dominant generation passed on?

Industry observers note that A rural sociologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1991 warned of big changes. Professor Tom Heberlein said “hunting as we know it” in Wisconsin could cease by 2050. He speculated the state might have to manage its deer herd with 100,000 well-trained animal control officers.

Heberlein, however, said his “straight-line projection” of declining hunter numbers wasn’t a prediction, given the unknowns of future technology, social trends, and natural events. Still, all evidence in 1991 revealed hunting interest had peaked with the then-middle-aged boomers and would only fall as they aged, became more urban and white collar, and led smaller, less structured families.

Most media outlets skipped such nuance and caveats as Heberlein’s warning generated national headlines and debates.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, wildlife agencies and universities wondered how institutions would fund habitat work, scientific studies, and hunting programs. They were learning firsthand the risks of relying on one type of crop for survival. In effect, hunting’s boom had relied on four specific elements:.

Recent findings suggest that A 2016 analysis by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service underscored the whitetail’s dominance. It highlighted that of the nation’s documented 13.7 million hunters in 2011, 79 percent (10.9 million) were deer hunters, primarily whitetail hunters. Although the accuracy of this oft-cited survey is unclear, it’s the best data we currently have for understanding national hunting trends.

According to recent reports, while hunting depended on whitetails for a species, it depended even more heavily on white males for participants. Roughly 10 percent of U.S. hunters today are female, but they form a slow-growing group with great “churn,” meaning they move in and out of hunting’s ranks at higher rates than males.

And of the 11.5 million Americans who hunted in 2016, 96 percent (11.1 million) were white.

In addition, even though states fund wildlife programs largely with license fees, sales of hunting licenses across much of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. are declining, even though few states have raised prices. Western states are keeping resident fees modest, but regularly jab nonresidents with license prices 10 times higher than what residents pay.

It has been revealed that the agencies’ other chief funding source is the federal excise taxes levied under the Pittman-Robertson Act on sales of ammo and firearms for hunting, self-defense, and recreational shooting. Many of today’s popular products didn’t exist when hunting boomed a half-century ago, and the P-R Act hasn’t been updated since Fred Bear and the archery industry persuaded Congress to impose excise taxes on bows, arrows, and accessories in 1972. Therefore, sales of scents, decoys, ATVs, tree-stands, hunting optics, rangefinders, trail cameras, ground blinds, game calls, GPS-driven smartphone apps, and high-tech clothing and footwear don’t -contribute to conservation.

Sources indicate that despite the challenges, I’m hopeful for the future of post-boomer hunting. Today, many younger hunters are just as hardcore as any grizzled boomer. Serious hunters, no matter their age, aren’t easily discouraged. We boomers eagerly toughed out state-mandated age requirements, some of which still stand, that forbade youngsters to hunt until ages 12, 14, or 16. And some fathers didn’t welcome boomers to deer camp until high school or after.

Industry observers note that “It was an honor to finally go to deer camp at 17 or 18,” says Rich Stedman, a rural sociologist at Cornell University and chairman of the school’s Department of Natural Resources and the Environment. Even though Stedman is a Gen Xer by two years, he hunts mostly with an older generation.

“There was something masculine about an early-1980s deer camp,” Stedman notes. “I was finally grown up enough to hunt with the men who survived a world war and the Great Depression. The boomers’ parents had a sense of optimism, a deep belief they could do the hard things. In comparison, our lives were relatively easy, so when we finally got to hunt with them, we tried hard to make the grade.”.

Stedman and his group cherished deer camp, and he laments the fading -multigenerational-​deer-​camp traditions but says it’s not the last institution that hunting will spawn, alter, or abandon.

Industry observers note that “I still feel connections to our camp, but I’m also haunted by its ghosts,” Stedman says. “It’s the repository of many stories that make you who you are. The flip side is that almost all those men are now gone. It’s time to make newly introduced memories, but I can’t make my kids see deer camp through my eyes. They don’t buy into challenges I welcomed. New things jar some of my traditions, but that’s how things change.”.

Industry observers note that will hunting’s younger generations find ways to fund the nation’s conservation programs with fewer hunters? Will they agree to pay more themselves, lobby for broader funding systems, or insist on both? Stedman, Caren Cooper, and other Cornell researchers found in 2015 that hunters, bird-watchers, and other nature-based outdoor recreationists were four to five times more likely than nonrecreationists to donate to conservation and wildlife initiatives.

Sources indicate that even so, Congress and voters haven’t tried to expand the Pittman-​Robertson Act beyond ammo, firearms, and archery for more than 50 years. Likewise, bird-watchers and other “nonconsumptive” recreationists fight suggestions to include binoculars, birdseed, bird feeders, or camping gear in the P-R Act.

It has been revealed that future generations of hunters might also have to broaden their passions beyond whitetails, whose overabundance in many areas has caused extensive over-browsing for the past 20 years, reducing the land’s carrying capacity. Meanwhile, chronic wasting disease has increased slowly but steadily, and if researchers are right, CWD-infected herds will decline without reductions in hunting harvest.

According to recent reports, will hunters then focus more on small-game species? Yes, history suggests. Even though deer dominated the boomers’ era, most boomers learned the craft by hunting small game and “graduating” to deer. Not until whitetails became so numerous in the 1980s and ’90s did most beginners start with deer.

Most importantly, the hunting community will need to broaden its population. Family-​driven hunter “recruitment” has fallen short, claims Wisconsin’s Christine Thomas, former dean of the College of Natural Resources at UW Stevens Point and founder of the Becoming an Outdoors-Woman program. Thomas says programs like BOW help fill voids, and she predicts more women will populate hunting’s ranks. So does Linda Bylander, who coordinates Minnesota’s BOW program.

“Our students are typically women who are just getting done with young-child–rearing duties, so they’re often between 30 and 40,” she indicates. “They want to hunt, and they like the locavore movement.”.

Likewise, a 2020 nationwide study of university students found that potential hunters, compared to active hunters, were more likely to be women or racial/ethnic minorities and less likely to have social support for hunting.

It has been revealed that rue Mapp, founder and CEO of Outdoor Afro, and Jimmy Flatt, Lydia Parker, and Thomas Tyner, co-founders of Hunters of Color, are helping to drive the conversation. They say many Blacks, Hispanics, Native Americans, and members of other ethnic groups are intrigued by hunting. Few come from hunting families, however, so few can ask relatives or friends for help.

“If you separate people for one generation from anything, it’s hard for them to reacquire those skills,” Parker notes. “You can learn some things by reading and watching YouTube videos, but you need repetitive lessons with others who hunt regularly. By matching our members with mentors and trying to create surrogate families, we hope to get beyond the R3 programs. We want hunting’s participation rates to eventually match society’s demographics.”.

Mapp has similar hopes but emphasizes she doesn’t want hunting to be colorblind.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d like it to be an American quilt, where each person is a patch sewn together into one community,” she notes. “Hunting unites us.”.

Sources indicate that latest York’s Jim Tantillo is a baby boomer and Cornell University professor who teaches environmental ethics and history and the philosophy and morality of hunting. He thinks hunting will likely benefit from the many programs now trying to recruit hunters.

“These programs help us learn which paths are closing and which ones are widening for hunters,” Tantillo says. -“Banquet-​based fundraisers and the traditional hunter-education model are probably past their expiration dates. No one should’ve thought they’d work forever.

Sources indicate that “This perception that we need to recruit hunters is newly introduced, but hunting is as old as mankind,” Tantillo continues. “I’m optimistic about hunting because Americans always turn to it as a way to be in the outdoors. Each generation finds its way.”.

It has been revealed that this story originally ran in the 2021 Traditions issue of Outdoor Life. Read more OL+ stories.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • Sources indicate that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

Sources indicate that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

It has been revealed that in addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush stated, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

Industry observers note that the Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

According to recent reports, the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

Recent findings suggest that there were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition declared Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” mentioned Kerry Stauffer.

In a recent development, last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

It has been revealed that tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • It has been revealed that rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

It has been revealed that rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

In a recent development, despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he notes the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka aims to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.
