#9691. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3162 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures.
  • Industry observers note that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet.
  • Sources indicate that whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures. And as strange as it may sound, bass and deer are really very much alike, at least in the ways they respond to bitter cold weather.

Industry observers note that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet. However, bass do begin exhibiting changed behavior. Generally bass will drift away from the shallows and into deeper water as the thermometer falls because temperatures in the depths remain relatively stable on a day-to-day basis. Here, their metabolisms begin to wind down. The bass, therefore, do not require as much food intake to sustain various bodily functions. Consequently, these two alterations in their lifestyle can make them very tough to catch for all but the most experienced fishermen.

Sources indicate that whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself. Yet few people, aside from biologists, are aware that deer also eat less as extremely cold weather approaches. Chemical changes take place in their bodies, causing their digestive processes to switch to s-l-o-w. This, in turn, allows for the maintenance of various body systems at a greatly reduced rate of food intake.

In a recent development, another notable point to emphasize about the anatomies of whitetails is that their brains are comparatively small in relation to their overall body sizes. Therefore, the integrated nervous system coursing throughout their bodies is rudimentary at best. As a result, like most wild creatures that do not possess a sophisticated neural apparatus, their pain thresholds are quite high — making them relatively insensitive to bitter cold temperatures. Many hunters are not aware of this because for generations they’ve been led to believe that when the weather goes sour, deer can be expected to do this or that in order “to seek protection from the elements and be more comfortable.”.

According to recent reports, body comfort actually has little to do with their changed behavior patterns. After all, the northern boundary of the whitetail’s native range extends more than 150 miles beyond the United States/Canadian border to approximately 52° latitude. Anyone who has lived thereabouts can tell you that winter temperatures frequently average -20°. The wind-chill factor often makes it seem as cold as -75°. Therefore, it just doesn’t stand to reason that animal species such as whitetails would be native to such hostile climes were they not virtually immune to such weather.

We’ve even seen evidence of this immunity right on our southern-Ohio farm where it is not uncommon to experience at least several days of -20° temperatures each winter.

Industry observers note that behind my barn there is an old tractor trail that wends its way through a 40-acre oak forest. Numerous times, while hauling out firewood, I’ve seen deer bedded on nearby slopes. Often they reveal a thick dusting of upcoming-fallen snow covering their backs — the hollow hairs of their coats providing such superb insulation that their body heat is unable to escape. If I approach too closely, the deer will predictably rise to their feet, shake themselves like soaking-wet dogs and cause clouds of snowflakes to fly — then saunter off to other parts with an air of nonchalance at having been rousted from their beds.

If deer are able to adapt to such gelid temperatures so easily, why is it then, that legions of otherwise knowledgeable hardworking hunters so often strike out when the freeze is on?

Say, for example, that you’ve been hunting in balmy temperatures for several days, have had the opportunity to look over a number of animals but haven’t seen anything you’d really be satisfied with. So you’ve decided to hold out a while longer, hoping you’ll eventually stumble onto “Mr. Massive.”.

Suddenly, you wake up one morning to the sound of icy sleet pinging against your bedroom window. Bounding from the rack, you are shocked to discover that the wind is whistling a siren song and that overnight the temperature has dropped 35°.

Recent findings suggest that after sitting on a stand for several hours that morning without seeing a thing, you look and feel like a popsicle. So you begin moving around — sneak hunting — but eventually conclude that the deer have vanished. By day’s end the temperature has fallen another 10°, a light skiff of hoarfrost blankets the ground and your expectations have long since dwindled. You’ve forgotten entirely about taking a nice buck this season and have begun thinking that if you can just manage to fill your doe tag you’ll be very very lucky.

The scenario is the bane of all hunters living north of the Mason-Dixon Line. Because it’s obvious that the deer couldn’t possibly have just disappeared from the face of the earth, the best prospect for success undoubtedly lies in learning more about their behavioral reactions to severe weather.

It has been revealed that one of the most telling clues to unraveling the mystery of their disappearance can be traced to changes in the whitetails’ body chemistry — the changes that cause them to require less food. Biologists say that this is an annual occurrence and that, like the rut, it is triggered by progressively shorter days and diminished periods of sunlight. Sometime around mid-November, the growth hormone thyroxin, which for the past eight months has been flooding the body, begins dissipating and will remain at a very low level until the following spring.

Industry observers note that this shoots down another popular myth about bucks not feeding much during the rut because they are so love struck. Actually, their reduced food intake can be attributed to a conservation measure on the part of nature. In other words, with each additional week of cold weather, food becomes less and less available so nature accordingly reduces the animals’ need for food by enacting significant changes in their body metabolisms.

Hunters should realize that, as the season progresses and as increasing numbers of severe polar blasts begin descending upon their regions, deer can be expected to move around less and less in search of food. The movements they do exhibit are no longer going to be concentrated during the traditional early and late hours of the day but during midday when it is likely to be warmer. Again, the deer are not seeking “comfort” but rather are conserving energy to more efficiently make use of the sharply reduced food supplies.

I’ve seen this happen with such consistency that I now almost consider it axiomatic. At our northern-Minnesota hunting camp, for example, members of our regular group begin bowhunting in October. We’ve learned from more than 80 years of combined experience that the odds of taking a whitetail early in the season are in our favor if we take up early-morning stands, nap during midday when deer are bedded, then resume our vigils late in the afternoon.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant.

Sources indicate that yet during the final days of the gun season in December, those in our party who still have not scored have entirely reversed their strategies. Now the order of the day, paradoxically perhaps, is to sleep late in the morning, wait on stand during midday, then quit early. There’s just not enough likelihood of seeing anything move — particularly at dawn’s first light — to justify the oftentimes agonizing ordeal of sitting as still as a statue in weather so bitter cold that it gnaws at your innermost fiber.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant. As far as they’re concerned, they want to be in the field every available minute. That’s fine and dandy but, if they want to maximize their chances for success, they should still be willing to make certain adjustments in the way they hunt.

According to recent reports, late in the season, and particularly when the freeze is on, they should stillhunt or sneak hunt early and late in the day when deer are most likely to be sequestered in their beds. During midday, hunters should play the waiting game on stand when deer are inclined to be traveling to and from feeding sites.

According to recent reports, but where, exactly, do the deer go when the bottom falls out of the thermometer and ice storms or sheets of wind-driven sleet are lashing the countryside? The three-pronged answer to this is thick cover on a protected south-facing slope in a low-elevation area of terrain.

Two of the most desirable types of thick cover are dense stands of head-high honeysuckle and nearly impenetrable pine plantations. The pines are most often thickets of immature trees that have their whorls of branches close to the ground.

Recent findings suggest that in the face of adverse weather, deer retreat deep into such seclusions where they can wait out the ensuing tempest. Again, trying to stay warm or achieve some other comfort level has little to do with their evasive behavior. Windy stormy weather makes whitetails extremely restless and nervous. By their very nature, whitetails are already hypertensive and are extremely paranoid creatures. When they’re no longer able to detect, classify and catalog sounds and scents because of the competition from noisy winds and erratic air currents, they waste no time finding a place where they can maintain a low profile. Therefore, rather than allowing themselves to remain vulnerable by bedding on their customary hillside benches and ridgelines, they retreat into deep thick cover. This not only helps to block the wind but perhaps also gives them the feeling that hiding from ready view somewhat compensates for their impaired senses.

Once, for a period of several days in the dead of winter, I had the opportunity to watch an eight-point whitetail buck in a fenced enclosure. This was a wild deer that had recently been captured by biologists for use in various nutrition studies. Its temporary fenced-in home was five acres of relatively open hardwood forest with scattered swatches of second-growth ground cover here and there.

It has been revealed that whenever the weather was warm, sunny and there was no wind, the buck had a particular place it liked to bed. The deer could see in every direction from the high hammock. Yet whenever a frontal storm system moved through the region and the wind began howling, the deer quickly vacated its usual turf. It always went downhill into a little pocket of thick multiflora rose — the only significant cover in the compound — and buried itself right in the middle.

One day as snow clouds scudded against an ominously gray sky and ice-riddled branches creaked in the wind, I watched in amazement as the buck laid on his belly for long hours, his front legs outstretched and his chin resting on the ground. Yet when the wind occasionally intensified with its typical freight-train drone, or an ice-laden branch suddenly crashed to the ground, the buck’s head would instantly come up, swiveling in all directions. Assured that nothing was on the prowl, the buck would then quickly duck back down again. Moments later his head would be up, down, then back up again. Just observing all that nervous energy and pent-up anxiety exhausted me — under these conditions the buck’s entire personality was like a violin string about to snap.

Industry observers note that I’m confident that the penned buck would have liked to have had access to much thicker deeper cover to increase his feeling of security. I’m also certain that unconfined deer in their native habitat behave much the same way when the freeze is on. Moreover, a biologist at the research station told me that during one terrible winter storm, the penned buck stayed put for four consecutive days until the weather finally abated.

Industry observers note that in addition to tangled jungles of honeysuckle and conifer forests, whitetails also like to retreat into swamps when the freeze is on. Because of the continually decaying organic matter, swamps are always warmer than other regions and this, coupled with the fact that they’re always found in low-lying terrain, keeps them somewhat sheltered from the brunt of the weather.

Recent findings suggest that however, without meaning to again kick the proverbial dead horse, deer don’t seek out swamps in order to stay warm. They go there because past experience has taught them that they’re not likely to bump into hunters in such forbidding territory and, similarly, a swamp is one place where they can continue to effectively rely upon their senses to forewarn them of impending danger.

Yet no matter what type of cover deer may elect to use for hiding, hunting them when the freeze is on can be extremely difficult because the animals’ minds and senses are so preoccupied with monitoring their immediate surroundings. But there are several tactics that seem to be far more productive than others.

Industry observers note that first, of course, pay attention to weather forecasts. Deer seem to have built-in barometers that give them advance notice when hostile weather is about to assault their regions. They take due advantage of this insight by stocking up on groceries, instinctively knowing that once the bitter weather strikes it will preclude safe traveling to and from feeding sites for several days. Then, immediately after the frontal system has passed and calmness again prevails, the deer come out of hiding and return to their favorite food plots. Consequently, stand hunting or sneak hunting — just before and immediately after a storm — are two key strategies no enterprising whitetail hunter can afford to pass up.

Cornfields can be prime places to try because, throughout the Midwest and the northern border states, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing as long as possible. In the past, it was either chopped or combined sometime in October or November. But with storage costs escalating like never before and future market prices uncertain, many farmers nowadays are leaving the corn in the field until such time as they have a specific need for it or until the price increases. Quite often this means as late as February.

Already-picked cornfields are also good bets because a substantial amount of harvest residue may continue to draw deer months after the corn has been combined. On our own cornfields we’re sometimes amazed to see a dozen deer at a time pawing through a foot of snow cover to find spillage.

In a recent development, I emphasize the importance of finding corn when the freeze is on because native wild foods are becoming more and more sparse with each additional week of winter weather. Other popular agricultural foods such as soybeans are rarely allowed to remain in the field beyond their peak harvest times, so corn is a deer magnet beyond compare.

Recent findings suggest that hunting during a storm can also pay off. The best opportunity occurs when the temperature does not fall dramatically. This usually means that the wind velocity will not be too fierce and any precipitation is likely to be in the form of huge wet snowflakes that begin clinging to cover like giant globs of cotton candy. Under such conditions, whitetails don’t seem to become as jittery and frantic about their safety and may continue to feed during midday periods. The fluffy snow itself may also pacify them just enough during nonfeeding periods so that they will remain tied to their usual haunts rather than diving headlong into thick security cover.

It has been revealed that any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground.

Industry observers note that conversely, hunting during the most ravaging freeze-outs offers the least chance of success. Now, patiently waiting on stand is inherently a futile endeavor. The animals simply will not come to you. It is necessary for you to go find them by prowling through swamps, honeysuckle or evergreens.

Sources indicate that never try to approach such cover on level ground. Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground. This will allow you to look down and through the cover and will make it far easier to spot bedded or sneaking deer.

Another option is to round up several pals and begin staging drives, particularly in the case of expansive pine plantations. Here is a unique situation, not unlike hunting rabbits, where the drivers themselves are likely to be awarded as many shots as the hunters placed on stand. The reason, as we briefly touched on earlier, is because deer that have retreated into the catacombs of thick cover are extremely reluctant to expose themselves, to travel great distances or to sever their close ties with that chosen cover where they’ve decided to holeup. As a result, a buck pushed out by a driver may chart a bounding weaving escape flight that actually takes him only a very short distance before he rapidly ducks back down to resume hiding.

Read Next: Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck.

Recent findings suggest that because the drivers are likely to see a good deal of shooting, those hunters placed on stand should use portable tree stands situated as high as practical so they are not in the direct line of fire of their approaching partners. Also — and this cannot be emphasized too strongly — every hunter participating in such a maneuver should be fully clad in fluorescent orange clothing and should maintain loud voice contact so everyone is well aware of each other’s location.

When hunting during freezing stormy weather, wise garment selection also requires careful thought. For sneak hunting or stillhunting, wool is always the best bet because it is noiseless when the fabric grates against brambles and brush. But when toughing out long hours on stand, I rely exclusively upon down-filled duds and bundle up like a snowman.

Sources indicate that I’d be the last to say that hunting deer when the freeze is on is purely enjoyable. Human beings just weren’t designed with bitter-cold weather in mind. But when such conditions prevail, any hunter can indeed fill his tag. Just keep in mind the changed behavior the animals are certain to begin exhibiting and plan your strategy accordingly.

This story was originally published in the November 1987 glitch of Outdoor Life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people.
  • Sources indicate that but getting to the trail takes more than a dream.
  • Sources indicate that through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people. Spanning 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada, the trail offers the opportunity to step away from everyday life, immerse yourself in the outdoors, and experience something that can be difficult to put into words.

Sources indicate that but getting to the trail takes more than a dream. For many aspiring thru-hikers, the financial commitment is one of the biggest barriers. Between gear, food, transportation, and the ability to step away from work for several months, the cost of a thru-hike can put the experience out of reach before someone even takes their first step.

The PCT Grant was created to help change that.

Sources indicate that through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. Its mission is to make long-distance hiking more accessible by easing the financial burden and giving someone the opportunity to pursue an experience they might not otherwise be able to afford.

At its heart, the program is about expanding access to the outdoors and recognizing that the transformative experiences found on trail shouldn’t be limited to those who can afford them.

Sources indicate that 2026 was the first year the PCT Grant came to life and chose its first recipient to take on thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. That person was me! The face behind the screen: Cappy. Post trail, I have joined the PCT Grant Committee to spread some magic with hopes of creating that same opportunity for others.

According to recent reports, receiving the grant was a lifeline. It wasn’t just financial support; it was the difference between being able to pursue this dream and having to put it on hold. It gave me room to take a chance on myself and say yes to an experience that changed the way I see what’s possible in life.

As this year’s recipient, I experienced firsthand what this kind of support can make possible. The trail taught me a lot about the power of choice and trust. The power of choosing something before knowing exactly how it will unfold, doing it scared, and learning to become comfortable with the uncomfortable.

Spending five months on trail offered so much more than the physical accomplishment of a thru-hike. I discovered how much we are capable of when we give ourselves the opportunity to find out. This trail changed my life, and it will continue to do so.

As the program enters its second year, the focus is on growing awareness, strengthening community support, and building a foundation for future recipients.

According to recent reports, presently, the grant is funded to support one hiker annually, with a longer-term vision of expanding its reach and helping more aspiring thru-hikers access the trail. From our fundraising efforts (a post trail Q&A with Cappy and other media platforms helping to spread the word) we have raised enough money to fund a second hiker this coming year.

Industry observers note that donations play an crucial role in making that possible. Every contribution helps sustain the program and move it closer to supporting additional hikers in the years ahead. We want to continue to grow this program so that even more hikers can set foot on the trail.

According to recent reports, applications for the 2027 PCT Grant are open through January 31, 2027. If you’re a Washingtonian between 18 and 33 with a dream of hiking the PCT, this could be an opportunity to make it happen.

And for those who have already experienced the magic of the trail, consider helping someone else get there.

Help make the next journey possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • Sources indicate that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • Recent findings suggest that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

Sources indicate that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

Recent findings suggest that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He stated climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

In a recent development, the Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

According to recent reports, “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

According to recent reports, this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” remarked Kondrashkin.

Sources indicate that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

In a recent development, on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#9682. Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1109 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like.
  • It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change.
  • Industry observers note that but it’s not just in my area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like. When I was a kid, more than 1 million hunters would enter the woods and hunt Pennsylvania’s opening day of rifle season. In my heavily populated area, I always saw a lot more hunters than I did deer.

It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change. The deer population was skyrocketing and it hasn’t slowed down. Paired with a decline in the hunting population, I’ve experienced the highest deer numbers of my life recently.

Industry observers note that but it’s not just in my area. The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags. Tack on the crazy advancements in technology like cellular trail cameras, the latest crossbows, and even technologically-advanced compound bows, and I truly believe deer hunting has never been easier than right now. Here’s why that’s a good thing — sort of.

According to recent reports, across the whitetail’s range, populations are at an all time high. That’s not just my opinion — it’s fact.

Sources indicate that “There are between 30 to 35 million whitetails in the U.S. right now,” indicates Kip Adams, chief conservation officer for the National Deer Association. “That’s a crazy number of deer on the landscape. And, the harvest data is backing that up. Nationally, we’ve only surpassed three million bucks harvested annually four times in the last century, all of which occurred within the last five years. We also have the best age structure in the last 100 years. So we’re killing more bucks, and older bucks than ever before.”.

The good news here is that the increasing population has been met with increases in opportunity from the tag allocation side, and the harvest data proves those opportunities are working.

Recent findings suggest that “We have expanded seasons across the board, higher bag limits than any point in the last century, and more advanced weapons to fill those tags,” states Adams. “If you can’t shoot a deer today, you just really aren’t trying very hard.”.

Now, before you go grabbing your pitchforks because you’re still sitting on a pile of tags this season, it’s worth mentioning that Adams and I both agreed that it’s never been easier to kill any deer, but we’re certainly not implying it’s easy to kill a specific deer.

Industry observers note that it’s also worth noting that certain areas across the whitetail’s range have seen a decrease in opportunities as diseases like CWD and EHD have impacted herd numbers, and habitat loss continues with urban expansion. But, for most of the whitetail’s range, opportunities abound.

According to recent reports, I’ll be the first to admit I love my cell cameras. I check them almost too often this time of year, but that immediate satisfaction and data grab is addicting. And, that data has helped me dial in the movement patterns of the deer herd in my area based on weather conditions in ways that standard SD card cameras couldn’t. That information, when applied correctly, makes filling a tag substantially easier than just guessing and trying to get lucky.

Recent findings suggest that take the buck my father tagged last year for example. We had gotten a few photos of him in velvet, keying us in on the area he was using. After planning to stay out of the area and wait for mid to late October when the buck started hitting scrapes, we sat back and waited. Around Oct. 21, we got our first photo of him in the area. And he stayed consistent for three days, hitting the scrape every evening in daylight. On the fourth night, we went in, set up, and a shot opportunity presented itself.

Sure, the stars had to align and the conditions had to be just right for that pattern to exist, but without the technological advancements to trail cameras, I don’t know if we would have gotten a chance at that buck.

Tack on the advancements in our gear. From compounds to crossbows, inlines to straight-walls, and even modern cartridge design, we’ve never been better equipped to shoot deer with more accuracy and efficacy.

“Almost all states in the whitetail’s range allow crossbows for everyone now,” Adams says. “Plus, more and more states that used to be shotgun only are now allowing straight-wall cartridges or inline muzzleloaders. All of those additions make it easier for hunters to fill their tags.”.

Industry observers note that while the pros speak for themselves, the cons come down to more of an opinion than anything rooted in fact. I have to wonder what all this ease is doing to the heritage of hunting. Hunting was never about being easy, in fact, I’d argue the opposite. It was about the thrill of the chase, the reward of filling your tag after a long season, putting your woodsmanship to the test and coming out on top, and the conservation of one of America’s most valuable resources.

I grew to love hunting because it was challenging. I was unsuccessful a lot, which put a fire in my belly to learn more, hunt harder, and find a way to be successful through the lessons I learned along the way. I wonder if kids like me are getting the same experience, and what the hook for them might be if not.

In a recent development, there’s also the ethical dilemma that an easier hunting experience brings. From the ethics and fair-chase argument relating to cellular trail cameras, to the liberal weapon usage and even baiting tactics in certain states, I fear we’re very close to crossing the line into an unfair advantage over our quarry, if we haven’t gotten there already.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

It has been revealed that it’s up to us as the hunters, and up to the states to decide how much is too much of a good thing. And as the deer populations continue to expand, I personally don’t see a world where the states are the ones that are going to draw the line. So, this season, as you continue to chase that substantial buck or a nice doe for the freezer, ask yourself where you plan to draw the line. And, feel free to join me in wondering how it’s still possible to struggle to fill a tag from time to time.

  • In a recent development, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

In a recent development, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Recent findings suggest that neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

Sources indicate that the Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Recent findings suggest that kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line right now being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Sources indicate that simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his looks while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#9675. Latest Update: Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (916 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk.
  • Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.
  • As I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk. At least 9 hours, too, which was way more than I had been getting.

Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.

As I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew. The girl was my age, and we discussed the Camino ending and what our lives would be like once we returned home. She was studying to be an actress and wanted to do so for the passion of it and to help people, not for the money or to be famous. She held many side jobs as a way to pay for her education and dream, one of them being teaching theater to children in a church. She spoke of the importance of giving young people a spiritual outlet, in whatever way felt best to them.

Sources indicate that the conversation then turned to my job and coaching. After telling her I help people find holistic balance in their life, she curiously asked me:.

“How do you find balance in your life?”.

This started a beautiful conversation about how we each live our lives, the things we prioritize, and our outlook on happiness and peace. A girl I’d met only a few days prior suddenly felt so familiar.

But then up ahead, I saw the brothers.

I yelled to them, and they waited for me to approach. With hugs and excitement, we all decided to go to a local restaurant, A Garnacha, for traditional Galician pulpo (octopus).

With three orders of pulpo in front of us, we dove into the tentacles with the toothpicks we were given as utensils. Not many words were stated as we devoured our plates. The boys asked if I liked it, and the best I could say was,.

“No es mi favorita, pero me gusta.”.

Sources indicate that for the first time in the whole Camino, the three of us walked together. Of course the Italian brother walked ahead, but we were still in close proximity.

The three of us dropped our packs at a pilgrim rest area, and ended up spending over an hour there.

We sang for the pilgrims that passed.

We laughed while we rested all together.

According to recent reports, my Argentinian brother and I were shocked by the fact that our Italian brother sat for that long. Having just bought his plane ticket home, he was feeling the weight of the Camino ending and wanted to slow down over the next few days.

He compared it to the last piece of pizza, and how you want to savor every single bite.

We were all savoring each moment together like it was the last piece of pizza.

In a recent development, the last part of the walk we did independently. I came up to a stream with a beautiful stone bridge over top. I took the moment to stop and be still, watching the ripples of the water reflect on the bridge. I pulled acorns out of the cold water and made a game of throwing them at a rock.

Simplicity. That’s what I love about this lifestyle, and something I will greatly miss.

When I arrived in the town of Arzúa and made it to the municipal albergue, Xunta de Galicia Arzúa Pilgrims Hostel, I showered and collapsed on my bunk.

In a recent development, my Italian brother came and got me once our Argentinian brother arrived, and we all walked to a restaurant in search of Galician barbecue. They were out of the barbecue we were looking for, so we ordered almost the entire menu instead.

Homemade croquettes, pimientos de Padrón (peppers), mixed salad, raxo, and milanesa de pollo.

There was not a crumb left. We got cheesecake and flan to top it off while the boys talked about the intersection of futbol and politics. I completely zoned out and started to see just how tired we all were.

That became quite evident in the street as we walked to find gelato. There was so much giggling and play, especially because we were delusional with exhaustion. But at one point, I walked behind the two of them as they were carrying on and thought,.

“I love these two so damn much.”.

And with a generous cone of gelato before bed, we all crashed for our last massive day.

Since completing her flip-flop at Springer Mountain, she has crafted her lifestyle to travel full-time and serve others within her passion of holistic health. This walk is another step into the unknown to embark on "A Saunter of Spirit" as she raises awareness for mental health through raising money for Hike For Mental Health. #9672. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • It has been revealed that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sources indicate that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

It has been revealed that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sources indicate that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Industry observers note that after 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

According to recent reports, several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

Recent findings suggest that “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

Recent findings suggest that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s blueprint to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Recent findings suggest that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

Recent findings suggest that “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

It has been revealed that in the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

Sources indicate that “Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

In a recent development, “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

It has been revealed that the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

In a recent development, rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

According to recent reports, strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

It has been revealed that strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

In a recent development, on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he claims:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

Recent findings suggest that the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#9670. ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (600 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer.
  • “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life.
  • It has been revealed that it was clear this was the season to try to kill him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

“We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”.

It has been revealed that it was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

According to recent reports, “I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”.

The Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

“The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack says. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”.

Zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

Industry observers note that “When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”.

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he indicates.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

“It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack notes. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”.

In a recent development, the deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

Recent findings suggest that although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” states Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”.

#9666. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1961 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • According to recent reports, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a new route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

According to recent reports, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a new route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential newly introduced line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Sources indicate that beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

Sources indicate that they climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

It has been revealed that they called their fresh line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Sources indicate that later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Sources indicate that three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

It has been revealed that one thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

It has been revealed that can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

It has been revealed that the two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Recent findings suggest that here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

At the moment, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

How many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

It has been revealed that during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive significant walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Recent findings suggest that some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

Industry observers note that the granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

It has been revealed that you climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

Sources indicate that there were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

In a recent development, at the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

According to recent reports, all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

Recent findings suggest that as in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

The most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a fresh route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road.
  • While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat issues, the recent development is creating even more consternation.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s unprecedented,” claims Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat issues, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

According to recent reports, “It’s unprecedented,” claims Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”.

The proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

The hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves claims.

Recent findings suggest that the Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, says Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner announced another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves says, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”.

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

In a recent development, the road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has mentioned he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”.

#9661. Latest Update: Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (794 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • Industry observers note that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

Industry observers note that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

In a recent development, the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

The accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police mentioned the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

It has been revealed that avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident indicates that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

In a recent development, the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

According to recent reports, fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the massive powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them initiative to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) indicates low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

In a recent development, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps shows remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

💡 Key Takeaways
